Two emerging tick viruses that can be deadly are spreading in the US

New Scientist August 20, 2026

Two tick-borne viruses – Heartland virus and Bourbon virus – have killed at least seven people in the US so far and appear to be spreading. Nebraska has just become the ninth state to detect one or both viruses in local ticks. New York also recently reported its first case of Bourbon virus in a person.

“Are these viruses going to keep expanding in ticks? Are we going to see more and more cases of human infections? These are questions that a lot of my colleagues and I are wondering about,” says Joseph Fauver at the University of Nebraska Medical Center.

Why Lyme disease and other tick-borne conditions are on the rise

Heartland virus was first reported in 2012 and Bourbon virus in 2015 after they were discovered in people who had become severely unwell or died after being bitten by ticks. Since then, they have been found to be transmitted by lone star ticks (Amblyomma americanum), named for the white, vaguely star-shaped spot on the female’s back.

Advertisement

Historically, lone star ticks were only found in south-eastern states of the US, but they have been pushing further north and west due to factors like climate change and reforestation of previously cleared areas.

Heartland virus or Bourbon virus, or both, have been found in lone star ticks in Missouri, Kansas, Illinois, Alabama, Georgia, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia. These ticks also recently became established in Nebraska, leading Fauver and his colleagues to investigate whether they have brought the viruses with them.

Free newsletter

The team analysed more than 7000 lone star ticks collected by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services from multiple locations across the state between 2022 and 2026. Both viruses were detected in ticks from Sarpy County, and Heartland virus was found in ticks from Richardson County. These are in the south-east of Nebraska, suggesting lone star ticks migrated from neighbouring Missouri and Kansas.

At this point, no one in Nebraska is known to have contracted these emerging viruses from tick bites. However, there is a “very real possibility” that human infections have occurred and gone undiagnosed, says Fauver. This is because the symptoms can be mistaken for those of other tick-borne illnesses or non-tick-related viruses, he says. Common symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, loss of appetite, muscle or joint aches and nausea.

Research suggests that only a small proportion of people who become infected with Heartland virus or Bourbon virus become severely unwell. Analysis of blood samples collected from hundreds of people in Missouri have found that almost 1 per cent have neutralising antibodies to Heartland virus and Bourbon virus, indicative of previous infections. “But it’s not like 1 per cent of people in Missouri have had these illnesses,” says Fauver.

There are no commercial tests for Heartland virus or Bourbon virus, so they are only detected when blood samples from hospitalised patients are sent for analysis at specialised laboratories, like at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Lyme disease is becoming increasingly common across the world, with warming temperatures one possible culprit for ticks spreading to new regions

Heartland virus is named after the Heartland Regional Medical Center in St. Joseph, Missouri, where it was first discovered in blood samples from two men who were hospitalised with severe illness after being bitten by ticks on their respective farms. Both men recovered, but one reported ongoing fatigue and headaches for years afterwards.

Since then, more than 80 people have been found to be infected with Heartland virus in central and eastern states of the US, and at least four have died. The most recent death, reported last October, was that of a 32-year-old Connecticut woman who had been exposed to ticks on a recent hiking trip. She died of a cardiac arrest, with an autopsy finding Heartland virus in her brain.

Bourbon virus is named after Bourbon County, Kansas, where the first known case of a human infection occurred in a man who noticed a tick on his shoulder after working outdoors on his property in 2014. He died soon afterwards from multi-organ failure. Since then, Bourbon virus has been detected in a small number of other people, some of whom have died.

New York, which is being increasingly colonised by lone star ticks, recently reported its first human infection with Bourbon virus. A man in his 60s contracted the virus after being bitten by multiple ticks while working outdoors on Long Island, which is particularly affected. The man, who recovered, was discovered to have Bourbon virus after a sample of his blood was sent to the New York State Department of Health by a research team led by Luis Marcos at Stony Brook University in New York.

“Bourbon virus is likely more prevalent than we think in our region and other cases are likely not being diagnosed,” Marcos said in a press release announcing the case last month. Heartland virus has also been detected in a small number of people in New York who have become unwell following tick bites, with the first case occurring in 2018.

“I think it’s a reasonable deduction that as lone star ticks expand their range, more and more people are at risk of getting exposed to Heartland virus and Bourbon virus,” says Fauver.

Mice overcame a Lyme disease infection after being given an antibiotic that is often used for pneumonia, and its effect on their gut microbiomes was negligible

Lone star ticks feed on animals like white-tailed deer and raccoons that have been found to have antibodies to Heartland virus and Bourbon virus, suggesting the viruses may continuously cycle between the ticks and these animals, says Fauver. “But there’s still a lot we don’t know.”

Lone star tick bites are also known for causing alpha-gal syndrome, which makes people allergic to red meat, and ehrlichiosis, characterised by fever, aches and headache. Lyme disease, which has similar symptoms, is caused by the black-legged tick (Ixodes scapularis). Ehrlichiosis and Lyme disease can be treated with antibiotics, whereas there are no antivirals or other treatments available for Heartland virus and Bourbon virus.

Continuous monitoring of the viruses is crucial so people can take precautions to protect themselves, says Fauver. “We’ll be going back and testing these sites [in Nebraska] to see if the viruses continue to show up, so that public health communications can be made to folks in these areas,” he says. “Obviously, you always want to avoid tick bites, but if you know you’re in a hotspot area where these viruses are circulating, you might want to be extra cautious.”

Depression doesn’t shrink the brain like we thought it did

New Scientist August 20, 2026

For more than a decade, depression has been linked to a shrunken hippocampus, the main memory centre of our brain. But now, a study of more than 23,000 brain scans suggests this doesn’t stack up.

In 2015, a study of nearly 9000 people – the largest of its kind at the time – concluded that people with recurrent depression have smaller hippocampi. It also suggested that the area gets progressively smaller alongside a growing number of depression episodes, implying that the mental health condition may be responsible for this shrinkage, rather than a small hippocampus causing depression.

Alzheimer’s, stroke, depression: The preventative power of sauna

Now, Janine Bijsterbosch at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis, Missouri, and her colleagues have analysed brain scans from 23,417 participants in the US and the UK across six large-scale datasets, including the UK Biobank. The team used modern imaging techniques that weren’t available in 2015, says Bijsterbosch.

Advertisement

The researchers were surprised to find no significant link between depression – assessed via questionnaires – and hippocampal volume. “It is surprising [that] no [hippocampal] shrinkage was seen,” says John Fleming at Southern Colorado TMS Center. “This study is very important and tells us we still need to learn more about all brain regions and not take hippocampal shrinkage as a given.”

Free newsletter

The team did link depression to reduced grey matter volume or cortical surface area in the frontal cortex, the anterior cingulate and the insula. All three of these areas are involved in emotional regulation. The frontal cortex is also involved in judgement and self-control, while the anterior cingulate has been linked to decision-making and motivation, and the insula helps perceive pain.

“All of these [traits and conditions] are disrupted in depressive symptoms,” says Fleming. The reduced volumes may therefore help explain common depression symptoms, such as brain fog and pain, he says.

It is unclear why depression seems to affect these areas specifically. One possibility may be that areas like the insula have a high degree of neuroplasticity, which may make them more vulnerable to the stress of depression, says Bijsterbosch.

Bijsterbosch stresses that her team measured depression at only a single time point, while the 2015 researchers tracked the condition across multiple episodes. What’s more, most of the participants in the latest study had mild to moderate symptoms, so hippocampal shrinkage may occur in recurrent or severe cases, she says.

If the effects of depression on the brain are explored further, this could help us understand the link between the mental health condition and dementia, says Fleming. A larger brain can protect against cognitive decline – if you assume cognition diminishes at some threshold of damage, then a bigger brain is going to succumb later.

Drugs like psilocybin that induce psychedelic effects have shown promise for treating depression. Now, a review of the evidence suggests that they are effective, but no more so than traditional antidepressants

It is feasible that brain shrinkage due to depression could raise the risk of this decline, says Fleming. But dementia is an umbrella term for a range of complex conditions associated with reduced brain function. Many factors can be involved, including inflammation and sticky protein plaques and tangles in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease, he says.

If future research robustly links brain shrinkage to depression, transcranial magnetic stimulation – using magnetic fields to stimulate specific areas of the brain – has been linked to modest increases in volume, so it could be explored as a treatment, says Bijsterbosch.

“We hope that getting a clearer picture of the brain basis of depression will inform future work to understand individual differences and ultimately guide improvements in personalised treatment,” she says.

Nature Mental Health DOI: 10.1038/s44220-026-00680-y

NASA calls off rescue effort to save doomed telescope

New Scientist August 20, 2026

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is doomed to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in the coming months, after a high-risk effort to save it failed.

On Wednesday 19 August, NASA said in a statement that an ongoing issue with the LINK spacecraft, built by US start-up Katalyst Space, meant that an effort to dock with and boost Swift in orbit would no longer be attempted.

“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the statement. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting.”

Advertisement

SpaceX crash site on moon revealed by South Korean orbiter

LINK was launched in July on a mission to save Swift, a rapid-response telescope used to observe brief celestial events such as gamma-ray bursts. Swift has been steadily dropping in orbit since its launch in 2004 due to atmospheric drag. The $30 million rescue mission, designed and built in less than a year, was a last-ditch attempt to boost the telescope back into a higher orbit.

Soon after launching, however, LINK began to spin out of control. While Katalyst later stabilised the spacecraft, it was deemed to have used too much fuel in the process to make the boost possible.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“Katalyst designed, developed, and launched an experimental spacecraft to go after an ambitious mission on an aggressive timeline,” the company’s CEO, Ghonhee Lee, said in a statement. “We took on this high-risk, high-reward challenge and are proud of the milestones we reached along the way.”

LINK will still rendezvous with Swift, but will no longer attempt to grab the telescope with its robotic arms. That means Swift will have a limited amount of final observations it can do before it re-enters the atmosphere by the end of the year, with no replacement telescope currently in the works.

AI firms are watermarking generated text – here’s why it won’t work

New Scientist August 20, 2026

As AI chatbots have taken off, you have probably found yourself wondering whether a piece of text you are reading was written by a human or a machine. Now, in response to European Union legislation, many AI firms are adding watermarks to text, images and video created by their models with the aim of letting you do just that. The hope is that these watermarks will help stem the spread of misinformation and bring transparency to the use of AI, but experts point out that, at least when it comes to text, watermarking is unlikely to work.

The requirement to watermark is part of the EU’s AI Act, and came into force on 2 August. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is already watermarking images and audio, and says it plans to add text watermarking in future. Anthropic, the firm behind Claude, has announced that future models will watermark text. The AI Act allows a grace period for models that have already been deployed, but all models must provide watermarking by 2 December this year.

Why I have changed my mind about AI and you should too

James Padolsey at NOPE, an AI safety firm, says that while image and video watermarks are more reliable because they are composed of dense and multi-layered data, watermarks in text will always be more difficult to implement.

Advertisement

One approach to watermarking text is to apply a mathematically detectable pattern to the choice of words. Large language models like ChatGPT create sentences by appending whichever word is statistically most likely to come next. By varying this selection of words, perhaps by choosing alternately the most likely next word and then the second, in repetition throughout a sentence, models can embed a pattern without changing the overall meaning of the text. Under the AI Act, AI companies will be required to offer tools that can look for these patterns, allowing people to identify AI-generated text.

But Padolsey points out that these watermarking patterns are susceptible to deletion by even light edits. “It’s not useful, and the way that people are going to try and use it will be incorrect,” he says. To drive home his point, Padolsey has created an online tool called declaude, which takes AI-generated text and lightly changes it in such a way that existing AI detectors no longer work. The same process should work on watermarked text, he says.

Even without such tools, Padolsey says that some open-source AI models that don’t abide by the EU’s rules will always be available, because these aren’t controlled by any one tech firm. “Any bad actors will just use those. And they’ll probably be cheaper and easier to run,” he says. “If you’re a nasty individual or a bad actor and you’re trying to generate this stuff en masse, it’s not hard to do.”

Rogue hacking AIs have changed the cybersecurity landscape

“These rules will help people recognise when they are interacting with AI or when content has been generated or altered by AI,” says a spokesperson for the European Commission. “The adversarial robustness of marking and detection solutions must be assessed in terms of resilience to malicious behaviour, such as copying, removal, regeneration and modification attacks on the markings.”

While Padolsey’s concern is that the watermarks are easily removed, others are worried about false positives – when text is found to be AI-generated in error, or because a model had even a minor role in producing a piece of work. Peter Scarfe at the University of Reading, UK, says lots of companies have pitched products to his department claiming to be able to help spot student plagiarism, albeit using other methods than watermarking, while also including small print that says their systems shouldn’t be used to conclusively prove or punish incidents of plagiarism because they aren’t infallible.

“If it says there’s a 67.8 per cent chance that this text was generated in some way by AI, as an educator, how would I act upon that? I’m not really sure,” he says. “These systems don’t work perfectly, and because of that, they’re of limited use.”

Watermark-detection tools will work in a similar way and could flag text that is simply processed by AI, not just text entirely generated by it. A student could find themselves in hot water even if they only asked a model to scan their manually written work for grammatical mistakes prior to submission.

Scarfe says that AI can be used for a host of purposes and doesn’t inherently spread misinformation, so perhaps a blanket policy on watermarking is a blunt instrument, but points out that it can make mistakes and hallucinate facts, and can also be used to disseminate lies quickly – such as by powering disinformation bots on social media.

“Because these technologies came in so quickly, and they’ve accelerated so quickly, everyone in every area of life is kind of on the back foot,” he says. “[But] I don’t think [watermarking] is a magic bullet. I don’t think it’s going to suddenly solve what the EU maybe are hoping it’s going to solve.”

AI may blunt our thinking skills – here’s what you can do about it

But perhaps watermarks may just create enough friction that they will put a brake on some nefarious uses of AI, such as mass creation of social media posts pushing disinformation. Erman Ayday at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, says that even if removing a watermark takes a trivial effort, this can, over time, make certain kinds of misuse impractical.

“Anybody can tamper with the watermark if they spend enough time on it, but then, when you spend enough time on it, then maybe you should have just generated the content yourself in the first place, right?” says Ayday.

Mira Arif named one of two Waikato winners on YWCA Y25 list

New Zealand Herald August 20, 2026

Mira Arif (centre) with some of her family.

Mira Arif watched her mother help refugees from Syria resettle in Hamilton.

It has inspired the Waikato 22-year-old to advocate for ethnic minority communities and create a sense of belonging for them.

Today, Arif has been recognised in the YWCA’s Y25 programme and listed as one of 25 young wāhine and gender-diverse changemakers aged 15 to 25.

The Y25 is an annual programme that celebrates and supports young leaders doing incredible things for their communities.

Arif is one of two Waikato women featuring in the programme this year, alongside Nasrin Najafi, 19, who is also a youth champion for refugees.

Arif has advocated for diverse communities and young people through roles including vice-president of the Waikato Students’ Union and community liaison with the Electoral Commission.

But the role that shaped her most was being a youth worker at Shama Ethnic Women’s Trust and Refugee Orientation Centre.

Born and raised in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, Arif was 12 when she moved to Hamilton with her family in 2016.

She is the youngest of six siblings, some of whom were already at university in New Zealand. As her parents got older, they decided to resettle in Hamilton and be closer to immediate family.

But the move wasn’t easy; it came with language barriers and cultural differences she hadn’t experienced before.

“In the United Arab Emirates ... everyone looked like me, and then moving to Hamilton [and they didn’t],” Arif told the Waikato Herald.

At the time, she felt they were “one of the first Arab families” in the city.

Her father is from Iraq and her mother is Syrian-Egyptian.

“I didn’t really understand what it meant to exist as, like, the person I am with my cultural background when I was placed in a society where no one looked like me.

“It was quite difficult for me.”

She felt “exposed to a completely different world”.

Until she left the UAE, she didn’t realise how privileged she was to have lived there.

“Like economically, and socio-economically, just everything. [From] the type of people, the culture, and the traditions, it was very different [in New Zealand].”

Homelessness was a sight she wasn’t used to.

“You ... can clearly see the imbalance.”

Something that made the move harder was not being able to rely on her parents, though Arif said it wasn’t their fault.

“They were trying to cope with their own set of barriers, like having poor English.

“It was like a fend-for-yourself type of situation ... but we all struggled.”

When the family found their footing, her mother started working for the Red Cross, helping Syrian refugees resettle in Hamilton.

That exposed Arif to “next-level hardship” among different communities.

“They were coming with a completely different set of traumas.”

That planted the seed for Arif’s passion for advocating for minority communities and creating a sense of belonging.

She said she wanted to “minimise the poor experience” people faced when moving to Hamilton as refugees.

“Just realising how much support is needed, especially for the young people within those communities, to feel like they’re not alone in this, is my passion.”

She said the ethnic minority experience could not be “dialled down to a singular struggle”, and advocating for those communities meant understanding that.

There were different levels of struggles, including family and sexual violence, and cultural and linguistic integration into society.

Arif wants to make sure that young people feel heard.

“Asking us what we think and then you’re given opportunities to speak, but there’s a big difference between, I guess, being heard and being listened to.”

She is still figuring out how to “tangibly make a difference” for youth.

Her advocacy work now sits alongside a legal career.

She was recently admitted to the bar as a barrister and solicitor of the High Court, and currently works as a governance graduate at Auckland Council.

She said she had seen first-hand how much knowledge minority communities hold compared to “formal institutions”, though it was easily overlooked.

Her passion is to “close that gap”.

“[And] not just having our ethnic communities consulted with, but really having their lived experiences be able to shape the decisions that will ultimately affect their lives.”

When asked about her Y25 win, and what positive change she wants to be known for, she said, “I don’t want to spend the rest of my life being the person that helps communities become better at complaining.

“I want to help build communities that don’t have to complain to be heard.”

Malisha Kumar is a multimedia journalist based in Hamilton. She joined the Waikato Herald in 2023 after working for Radio 1XX in Whakatāne.

The Maccanico family had decided to cut their summer camping holiday in Mount Maunganui short, with bad weather coming.

But a campground staff member convinced the Aucklanders to stay.

Two days later, a landslide at the camp took the lives of teenagers Sharon Maccanico and her boyfriend, Max Furse-Kee.

The 15-year-old Pakūranga College students were the youngest of the six victims of the Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park tragedy on January 22.

The family’s story was outlined in retired High Court judge Paul Davison’s review into the landslide for Tauranga City Council, which owns the iconic campground at the foot of Mauao.

The review, released on Wednesday, found the council “missed several opportunities” to evacuate campers in the 24 hours before the disaster – starting from when a red heavy rain warning was issued.

Davison described the landslide as “preventable” and found the council knew of the risk to the campground, but systemic failures meant this was not appropriately managed.

His report said Sharon and Max were holidaying in Mount Maunganui with Sharon’s parents, Carmine and Natallia Maccanico.

The family had planned to stay from January 17 to 29, initially camping in a tent on the ocean side of the park.

On January 19, strong winds and forecasts of heavy rain prompted Carmine to go to the campground office and cancel their booking.

“He was encouraged by a member of the office staff to stay, saying that although the weather forecasts were bad, rather than leaving and returning home, they had the option of renting a caravan or a cabin at the campground,” Davison’s report said.

They decided to rent a caravan until the storm passed, moving into one right beside the harbour amenities block.

They stayed in the caravan on January 20 and 21, when the worst of the forecast heavy rain arrived.

By the morning of January 22, the rain had stopped, and the family planned to move to a site away from the flooded areas.

About 7am, Natallia noticed the water around their caravan had turned brown and muddy.

An hour and a half later, she filmed muddy water and gravel from the slope above the amenities block and across the driveway.

The report recalled the blue skies that morning after the storm passed, but many campers had left or moved away from flooded areas, leaving the campground quieter than usual.

About 9.20am, Sharon and Max grabbed clean clothes and headed off to the amenities block to have showers.

Fellow camper Lisa Maclennan had also just gone in for a shower about then, and Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler and Måns Bernhardsson were also in the amenity block.

Shortly before 9.30am, a staff member heard a crack. They saw a pōhutukawa tree sweep down the block and watched the landslide strike the amenities block “like it was hit by a missile”.

The staff member ran to the slip and climbed on to the displaced roof of the building to help remove roofing iron. Another staff member called 111 and waded waist-deep into the mud, searching for people trapped in the debris.

He recalled Sharon’s mother screaming: “They’re both in there.”

The report said a distressed Carmine was on the roof, desperately searching for his daughter.

The staff member said twice the group fell silent to listen for sounds of anyone trapped by the landslide.

The first time, he was “fairly sure” he heard a muffled sound.

The second time, he heard nothing.

All six holidaymakers who were in or near the amenities building perished.

In a statement via police on January 30, Sharon’s parents described their daughter as “beautiful”, highly respected, and having a great sense of humour.

Natallia and Carmine said their hearts were “broken” by the loss of their daughter.

“One year ago, Sharon met the love of her life, Max. They very quickly formed a strong relationship.

“Max became a treasured part of our family, and he looked after Sharon and made her feel so special.”

A silver-linked bracelet Sharon wore, inscribed with “Max”, also helped play a role in formally identifying her remains at a Coroner’s Court victim identification hearing.

Her dance community remembered her as a gifted performer whose talent, passion and kindness left a lasting mark.

She joined Auckland’s RGD Studio in 2022 and became a core member of its top junior hip-hop crew.

At 12, she and her crew placed ninth at the Hip Hop World Championships in Arizona.

RGD Studio director Rebecca Gray described Sharon as a “rare soul” who was “exceptionally talented”, kind and inclusive.

Sharon was born in Italy and moved to New Zealand aged 8.

The Herald understands her parents have moved back to Italy.

In the week following the slip, Max Furse-Kee’s mother Hannah Furse released a statement via police that said the family took comfort in knowing he spent his final days with his girlfriend, whom he loved deeply.

Furse said Max was “suddenly and unimaginably taken from us”.

“He simply went to take a shower, in the wrong place at the wrong time,” she said.

Furse described Max as a “beautiful soul” who brought immense light, laughter and love to their lives, and she thanked those involved in the recovery effort.

He was remembered at a memorial service as a great friend who loved basketball. He was about to turn 16 and was excited about the prospect of getting his provisional driver’s licence.

Strong magnitude 6.7 quake rocks central Peru

New Zealand Herald August 20, 2026

The 6.7 magnitude quake struck near Upahuacho in Peru at 6am NZ time.

A strong magnitude 6.7 earthquake has rocked central Peru this morning.

The tremor struck 38km northwest of Upahuacho at 6am NZ time, according to the Honolulu Pacific Warning Centre.

There was no tsunami threat at this time, the centre said.

The United States Geological Survey said the quake struck at a depth of 66km.

The Peruvian Geophysical Institute (IGP) has recorded the quake as magnitude 7.2.

Local media are reporting it could felt a long way from the epicentre, including in Lima, the Peruvian capital.

Images broadcast by Peruvian media showed rocks and earth tumbling down hills around Coracora in Ayacucho region, the closest town to the epicenter, which has a population of about 10,000.

“The population has responded, they evacuated and took shelter,” the town’s mayor Yony Odon told state television in a telephone call, saying he was hopeful there was no major damage.

The tremor was also felt in Cusco, Arequipa and even Lima, although with lesser intensity, AFP journalists said.

One video posted to social media shows students and teachers at a school in the city of Cusco running out of buildings and sheltering on fields and sports facilities as the earthquake strikes, while another shows residents huddling in the street as the ground shakes.

Other videos filmed high in the Andes show dust rising from the mountains as a deep rumbling sounds in the background.

The earthquake follows two major quakes in the region since June: a double earthquake in Venezuela on June 24 that killed over 6,400 people and a powerful tremor in Colombia last week that left nearly 300 people dead.

Officials continue to work to find any sign of life in the Colombian rubble but hopes dwindle as the days go on.

Over 100 people are still missing and thousands of people have been injured in the 7.4 magnitude earthquake - the most powerful quake to have struck Colombia in nearly half a century.

Auckland Hospital’s near-constant overcrowding putting patients at risk, doctor says

New Zealand Herald August 20, 2026

Auckland Hospital is the country's largest hospital. Photo / RNZ, Marika Khabazi

By Keiller MacDuff of RNZ

An Auckland Hospital doctor says near-constant overcrowding in the emergency department is leaving staff demoralised and putting patients at risk, while a patient advocate says Health NZ data shows some EDs are in “a state of failure”.

The emergency department at the country’s largest hospital met the criteria for an “escalation pathway” at least once a day on most days in 2025, according to figures released to the Labour Party under the Official Information Act.

The information came in response to a question on the number of “code reds” across New Zealand hospitals, but Health NZ said every hospital had different triggers for code reds and the information could not be easily compared.

A spokesperson said Auckland Hospital did not have a code red scale, but instead used an “escalation pathway” which meant a clinical or operational response was triggered when the emergency department met one of three thresholds – if more than 30 people were waiting for sign-on (the time it takes for a doctor or specialist nurse to be assigned to a patient), if the ED was more than 120% over capacity or if four or more ambulances were unable to hand over their patient within 15 minutes.

Health NZ’s figures showed the ED breached its threshold for people waiting for sign-on at least once on 281 out of 365 days (77% of days), its ambulance escalation trigger on 286 days (79% of the year), and was more than 120% over capacity on 117 days (32% of the year).

A Health NZ spokesperson said it had no way of knowing how long the measures were exceeded on any day, nor did it have a record of whether the exceedances prompted any further actions.

Auckland Hospital emergency physician Dr Mike Nicholls said the ED was the canary in the coal mine.

“The emergency department is part of a complex healthcare system and it’s a useful way of looking at the healthcare system in total because often when things aren’t going well in other parts of the healthcare system, we see that in the emergency department.”

Nicholls said that while the data provided a good picture, it was not the full one.

For example, capacity breaches recorded when the ED was more than 120% over capacity but not by how much or for how long, or whether more than 30 people waiting meant 31 people waiting for five minutes or 50 people waiting for eight hours.

But there was no doubt the conditions posed a risk to patients, Nicholls said.

“Overcrowding in emergency departments is associated with increased harm for patients, including increased death. An escalation pathway is there to get everyone on the same page that we’re in a really risky situation.”

The situation was tough on staff, he said.

“I think everyone who works in an emergency department does so because they want to provide the best care possible. They’re really people who like to be challenged, but not necessarily in this way where the situation means it’s not possible to deliver the quality of care that would be possible were it not for those overcrowding issues.”

Nicholls said the problem became acute when overcrowding was not just for a day or a week or a month, but ongoing.

During January, February and June, Auckland ED had breached its wait-time threshold at least once almost every day (94% in January and 93% in February and June), while it breached its ambulance escalation trigger at least once on 94%, 96% and 93% of days in the same months.

Nicholls said the causes were complex, but boiled down to levels of demand versus resources.

“When you’re getting more than 120% occupancy frequently or the other findings ... most people would agree the demand is outstripping the resource and it’s throughout the healthcare system.”

He had not observed the same issues Christchurch Hospital was experiencing with patients treated in corridors but said there were “absolutely patients waiting in spaces that aren’t designed for high quality health care” and where it was not intended patients would be “for any length of time”.

“When people arrive in our emergency department, there’s people waiting for often quite some time – some hours at times – and we’re not able to deliver good care for them ...

“That’s a real problem for those patients and families, and it’s a real problem for staff as well because we know we’re not able to deliver the care people need. That’s really quite demoralising to witness people not getting the care we know they need.”

The Government’s six-hour target (for 95% of ED stays to be less than six hours) was “one way to look at a very complex system”, but “in an effort to simplify that information so it can be understood by a lot of people you lose something trying to reduce a problem to one number”, Nicholls said.

Even when EDs were making improvements on the target, that didn’t “change the fact we’re still having a lot of problems with overcrowding in our emergency departments. Both things can be true”.

Overcrowding exacerbated an already stressful situation, he said.

“It’s more stressful for me and I think I can speak for my colleagues, it’s more stressful for them and I think I can speak for patients and their whānau who are the most important people in the healthcare system – I think it is very stressful for people.

“By far the majority of the time, patients and family are really understanding and very kind to myself and colleagues, but sometimes the stress is too much for everybody and people do get upset.”

Health NZ group director of Auckland operations Dr Michael Shepherd said it was incorrect to characterise the measures being met or exceeded as “breaches” or to use them as measures of activity or performance.

The thresholds were “operational management tools” to assist staff, may have only been met for a short period of time, and indicated further action was required, not that the ED’s performance was impaired, he said.

Once the thresholds were met or exceeded, the response could include adjusting staffing levels and placement, prioritising workflow and reviewing admission processes.

“Like emergency departments across New Zealand and internationally, Auckland’s Emergency Department continues to experience significant demand,” Shepherd said.

Health New Zealand had implemented initiatives to improve patient flow, reduce delays, strengthen workforce capacity and support timely ambulance transfers, he said.

Patient Voice Aotearoa chair Malcolm Mulholland said the data showed emergency departments were in a “state of failure”.

“It shows patients aren’t being seen quickly enough, that there clearly are not enough beds and that ambulance ramping is becoming standard practice around the country.”

The situation could be worse for regional hospitals, which were sometimes forced to close the emergency department because of staff shortages, he said.

Association of Salaried Medical Specialists executive director Sarah Dalton said it did not matter how Health NZ classified the information, the system was clearly overwhelmed.

“Whether you call it a code red, a code black, an escalation point, a breach, what all of the data tells us and what our members who are senior doctors working in emergency departments tell us is that they are not appropriately resourced to cope with the level of need.”

Members also reported the vast majority of patients presenting at ED needed to be assessed at a hospital and sometimes admitted, she said.

“This isn’t just people going there instead of a GP. This is people who are sick enough that they should be seen at a hospital.”

It was frustrating to have the same conversations every year, Dalton said.

“It isn’t a snapshot, it’s an ongoing trend.”

“What’s the point of all of these statistics and measures if Health New Zealand and the Government aren’t willing to throw the resources that are needed at acute care?”

Whangārei stump grinder death: Kevin Barry pulled into spinning blade

New Zealand Herald August 20, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

An arborist removing tree stumps in a residential street was grabbed by his shirt sleeve and pulled into the spinning blade of the machine he was using.

Kevin Barry, who only months earlier had started work as a groundsperson for an Auckland tree-maintenance firm, never had time to save himself.

The 69-year-old died in April last year from unsurvivable head injuries.

A coroner said in findings released today that Barry appeared to have got too close to the spinning cutter wheel in the large stump grinder he was operating.

The speed at which he was pulled into it meant he was unable to activate the emergency stop on the remote-control unit before being incapacitated.

A member of the public found him lying critically injured beside his vehicle.

The same witness used the emergency stop switch to turn off the machine.

Another member of the public called emergency services, which provided advanced supportive care to the critically injured Barry, who was taken to Whangārei Hospital.

In findings released today, Coroner Ian Telford said Barry’s injuries were unsurvivable and he died in hospital on the evening of April 15 last year.

His daughter, Megan Barry, who shared his great passion for motorsport and speedway, told NZME her father was much more than the circumstances of his death.

She said on behalf of the family that while no report could bring him back, they were grateful the coronial inquest was over.

“The process has required us to revisit one of the most painful periods of our lives, and we are grateful that Kevin’s story has been carefully heard and considered,” she said in a statement.

As the family reflected on the findings, their focus remained on honouring his memory and the interests which brought him so much happiness.

He would always be remembered as a devoted family man, a loyal friend, and someone whose love of life, family, and motorsport brought people together, Megan Barry said.

“Motorsport was a significant part of his life, and Saturday nights at Western Springs Speedway were a treasured family tradition.

“The memories made there will always hold a special place in our hearts.”

She still heard his voice in moments when faced with a challenge or difficult decision, especially in her role as course clerk at Lucas Oil Auckland Speedway.

“I often find myself asking, ‘What would Dad do’?”

At other times, she could almost hear him saying one of his favourite phrases: “You bloody muppet”.

“It was classic Kevin, delivered with humour, warmth, and usually a lesson not far behind.

“Those words still make us smile and remind us of the man we miss every day.”

The family expressed their heartfelt thanks to everyone who had supported them.

“The compassion, understanding, and encouragement of our family, friends, and wider community have been invaluable and have helped sustain us through some of our most difficult days.”

Coroner Telford said the accident was a “stark reminder” that the dangers posed by the machine being used must never be underestimated.

Barry had travelled to Whangārei on the morning of April 14 last year.

He received training on the track stump grinder soon after starting the job and was assessed as competent to operate it.

The machine was controlled remotely and featured a rotating cutter wheel used to grind stumps.

Barry’s employer said he knew the machine well and could troubleshoot and fix mechanical problems.

He described him as a smart, physically fit worker who was careful and safety-conscious.

On arriving in Whangārei, Barry met a supervisor who reviewed the work and observed his operations.

No concerns were identified, Coroner Telford said.

The following morning, the supervisor carried out safety checks before Barry began removing two tree stumps on a grass berm.

He was wearing standard safety gear including a helmet, safety boots, hearing protection, face and visual protection and a long-sleeved, high-visibility top.

He had the remote-control unit around his neck.

Coroner Telford said consistent with his company’s lone worker policy, Barry was carrying a mobile phone he used to send photos and work updates.

About 20 minutes after he last used his phone at 5pm, he was found by a passerby, lying critically injured on the ground.

Contact the Open Justice team

A WorkSafe investigation found no breach of health and safety laws.

The machine and remote control unit were independently tested and found to be working as expected.

WorkSafe said in the absence of witnesses or CCTV, the scene photographs and Barry’s injuries provided the best evidence to establish what occurred.

It concluded that after the stump grinding was finished, Barry raised the cutting arm so the cutter wheel was clear of the ground.

Contrary to the required operating procedure, the cutter wheel was not disengaged but remained spinning while the stump grinder was manoeuvred into the position in which it was later found.

Coroner Telford said this placed the machine at an angle to the pavement edge and adjacent to Barry’s vehicle and trailer, parked nearby on the roadside.

“For reasons unknown, possibly while attempting to pass between the stump grinder and the parked vehicle, Mr Barry approached the area of the spinning cutter wheel.”

It placed him within the recognised danger zone, resulting in the fatal accident.

Coroner Telford said that while it was not possible to know precisely what happened, he accepted WorkSafe’s theory as the most likely scenario.

He recommended WorkSafe emphasise that tree work carried a high risk of serious accidents and that stump grinders were hazardous machines requiring appropriate controls and specialist training.

“I am satisfied Mr Barry was acutely aware of these hazards and was a careful and safety-conscious operator who was regarded as highly competent.

“Nevertheless, this tragic accident is a reminder that, even in the hands of skilled operators, the risks associated with this machinery remain significant and ever-present.”

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was previously RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

St Andrew’s College First XV chasing 35-year drought-breaker in South Island final

New Zealand Herald August 20, 2026

St Andrew’s College will be aiming to break a 35-year drought when their First XV take on Southland Boys’ High School in the South Island final on Saturday.

The winner will book a place at the Top 4 National First XV finals in Palmerston North next month, a tournament that St Andrew’s College has not been to since 1991 – when it was a single-sex school.

Among the names that went on to higher honours from that team is Glenn Delaney, a former professional who played in Japan and Europe before returning home to coach Canterbury’s NPC team. Delaney’s nephew, Zac Hoshek, could follow in his footsteps with a win on Saturday.

Willi Heinz, the school’s head rugby coach, says the team is aware of the history – but they’re not looking that far ahead.

“I know it’s a horrific cliché, but we just focus on the day ahead of us and challenge them to be really present through the schooling day and then when we turn up for training, we just rip into that,” Heinz said.

A former England and Crusaders halfback, Heinz is in his first year at St Andrew’s, having worked with Christchurch Boys’ High School last season. St Andrew’s beat CBHS in the Crusaders region final last weekend 33-17.

St Andrew’s, a co-educational private school since 1992, was excluded from this year’s South Island Boys’ School Competition, which pitted some of the South Island’s heavyweight First XVs against each other throughout the season. It was ultimately won by CBHS, who held off Southland Boys’ High School for the inaugural title.

Heinz believes there were pros and cons to not being involved in the new competition.

“I guess the benefit of being involved in a competition like that is you’re getting good, tough rugby every week,” he said.

“We had some challenges to deal with at the back end of the season. The way the draw worked out for us it means that going into finals we had a month without competition rugby, but that’s why we took the boys over to Australia for a couple of games.

“On the other hand, maybe some of those weeks have allowed us to freshen up a little bit where other teams have still effectively been playing almost every week.”

That downtime has allowed injuries to heal and St Andrew’s will go into the final with near-enough a full squad to call on – including rich front-row stocks.

“We’ve always talked about the way we train is the way we play and right from the start of the season, particularly with Owen [Franks, forwards coach] and lately Trent Harris, who’s taken over since Owen moved on to his Japanese stuff, was just the way that those boys set themselves up each week. They’ve battered the crap out of each other in training, to be honest. I think that’s created a really competitive edge amongst the forwards and it sets them up for game day,” Heinz said.

The experienced Heinz is now turning his attention towards how they can use that physicality against Southland Boys’.

“Just spending a bit of time looking at them this week, they’re a quality outfit, they’ve got threats right across the park. It’s going to be a hell of a challenge for our boys.”

For Southland Boys’, it may be a new opponent; in fact, some SBHS old boys wonder if the schools have ever played before – but this end of the season is very familiar. Winners of the Top 4 title in 2023, the Invercargill school finished third in the national finals last year and have now been in the past four South Island finals. They won the Highlanders regional final against King’s High School 49-15 in Invercargill last weekend.

Long-time coach Jason Dermody says this year has been a challenge with the extra SIBS fixtures.

“I think it’s helped in the way that you have to be better planned every week.

“We’ve planned most weeks pretty well. Not knowing the opposition and making the boys get up every week was tough. We thought we would have weeks where we could rest people, but that didn’t really happen. We played our best team week in, week out.

“The boys are pretty battle-hardened.”

Dermody says it had always been in the back of his mind that St Andrew’s would get right through.

“They’ve sort of timed their run as well. I know they went to Aussie for a 10-day tournament.

“They’ll be very difficult, especially at home as well. They’ve got a big crowd and they’ve got a lot of support, so we’re under no illusions about what we’re going into.”

Maintaining a standard like Southland Boys’ have managed takes careful planning as boys finish their schooling and new faces move into the top team.

“It’s a lot of hard work. We’re always looking at boys that would fit into our mould. We pick good people first before good players, and we make the boys buy into what we’re about. And if we don’t think they’re up to that, then we won’t pick them.

“We spend a lot of time with our boys, so we want to be around good individuals. We don’t really deal with any muppets. I haven’t got time to be dealing with people like that,” Dermody said.

The long, hard season has seen Dermody use 34 players this season, adding to the side’s depth for years to come. But this year is still the primary focus.

“Our goal from the start of the season is to be the best in the South Island. So, our goal is definitely to win on Saturday.”

Both sides wear a very similar kit – so one will need to wear an alternative. Dermody says he’s not sure who it’ll be, but he has an idea.

“It’s usually the home team.”

Mike Thorpe is a senior multimedia journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

China was making too many cars. They turned to Australia to offload them

Sydney Morning Herald August 21, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Holden, Ford, Toyota, Nissan, Mitsubishi. For years these are the brands which have dominated the driveways of Australian homes.

Now brands such as XPeng, Zeekr, Haval, GAC, Geely, Chery and Leapmotor are competing for customers – and you probably know someone who drives one, even if you don’t yourself … yet.

One in every three vehicles sold in Australia in the first six months of this year was made in China. There are at least 10 Chinese automotive companies selling more than 20 individual brands, mostly EVs and plug-in hybrids. And more are coming. Names such as BAW, Changan, Forthing and Nio, all hoping to make a mark in what is widely considered the most competitive car market in the world.

But none has yet made the impact of BYD, which launched in Australia with the hopeful moniker Build Your Dreams in 2022, before rebranding its vehicles with the shorter and more palatable initialism soon after. There was scepticism when, not long after launch, its executives told a packed media room that it would be a top-five brand in Australia in 2025, and then continue to grow. For a new brand with only a handful of models, it seemed incredible hubris. But in mid-year 2026, BYD is ahead of schedule.

The scale of the appetite for the Chinese auto giant’s cars was evident when the vast BYD Zhengzhou ship sailed into Melbourne in June, with almost 5000 vehicles on board the 200-metre-long floating showroom. BYD had mobilised the shipment in response to the demand for “greener” vehicles in Australia. The same month, the company sold almost 19,000 vehicles here – just 243 sales short of Toyota. The last time a brand beat Toyota in the monthly sales race was in May 2011 – and that was Holden.

BYD local chief operating officer Stephen Collins says technology is now a key factor being sought by Australian motorists, who were open to new brands who could deliver.

It hasn’t all been smooth sailing on BYD’s Australian ascent, though. The champagne that was no doubt flowing following the brand’s best-ever month in June would have quickly soured when, in July, it emerged that more than 1200 customers had been sold 2025-build vehicles, not the 2026 models they had paid for. A BYD spokesman was reported as saying it was due to an “administrative error”, and the company has since offered all those affected the option of a full refund.

In May, the federal opposition called for a security review into whether any Chinese EVs should remain on the list of taxpayer-funded cars available to parliamentarians, with opposition special minister of state James McGrath describing them as “effectively rolling Chinese data centres”.

Legacy brands are watching the newcomers in the Australian market. The local CEO of Korean auto giant Hyundai, Don Romano, bristles when asked if he is surprised at the speed at which BYD had grown here. “I think there’s a big difference between growth at any cost and growth organically,” he said.

Vice president of sales and marketing of Toyota, Australia’s best-selling marque, John Pappas says that something will have to give. “There are all these other brands coming, but the market itself is not growing. So it’s going to be a challenging environment for some of these brands to be sustainable,” he says.

BYD might be the headline act, but it is only the tip of a very long spear. Few brands demonstrate the automotive gold rush under way in China better than Dreame, a home electronics company most famous for robotic vacuum cleaners after launching its first stick vacuum in 2018. The brand claims that within the next 18 months, Dreame cars will be for sale in Australia – though details of the SUV range have yet to be revealed – with the brand exploring retail outlets such as Harvey Norman as a substitute for a traditional dealership network. The plan, presumably, is to allow you to buy a couch, a TV and a vacuum cleaner – and then the car you need to get them home.

“There are legacy brands who just believe their repeat customers are always going to be there. If we can come in and really showcase the value of our brand, there’s a gap there where we believe customers will transition through,” says Dreame’s Australian manager James Moore.

The speed of this change to our new-car market is staggering. In 2020, 30,000 cars sold in Australia were made in China (and in 2019 it was more like 17,000). Over the first six months of 2026, that number was almost 200,000. China is now the single biggest source of origin for vehicles sold in Australia, snapping a 28-year record held by Japan. Helping, too, is that brands like Tesla also source their vehicles from China.

Several events have driven this growth. Over the past five years here, international conflicts have spiked petrol prices, inflation-driven rate rises have hurt household budgets, government incentives have accelerated the adoption of greener vehicles, wait times for certain legacy manufacturers have spiralled, and the 2025 introduction of the ever-tightening New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (which fines brands that don’t meet it) has driven a move to rush EVs to market.

Meanwhile, a Chinese manufacturing glut, which has prompted authorities there to clamp down on new car-making facilities and price-cutting wars, inspired company executives to look outwards a few years ago. Europe and the US both have domestic automotive industries to protect. Australia does not, and so has some of the lowest barriers to entry on the planet. Gas meets match.

Mike Costello, an auto analyst at Cox Automotive and Manheim Australia, says that China had over-produced for its local market and started looking for export markets. “China leads the world in all things to do with electrification, and so they recognised that they could really steal a march on everybody as we moved into this new, electrified world,” he says. “They also knew that, through sheer economies of scale or through government help or through really low-cost manufacturing, they could get a leg-up on price as well.”

That, says Costello, is a critical point. Chinese vehicles are often cheaper than their rivals, sport more equipment and features on their cheapest, entry-level models and with world-class battery technology. For perspective, the Toyota RAV4 is one of the nation’s bestselling vehicles, and a plug-in hybrid version of this mega-popular SUV arrived in Australia in June. The cheapest version is $58,840 before any on-road costs. The similarly sized Starray from Chinese brand Geely is $37,490. Brand loyalty is suddenly rather expensive.

On the surface, the consumer benefits most. The arrival of this army of new brands is driving down prices significantly. But, says Costello, one of the few things not included in the sticker price of a new brand’s vehicle is the implied security of legacy.

“The one thing the Chinese brands don’t have is long-term proven residual values and long-term proven reliability in Australia. And that’s not to say that they won’t have those things. But if you buy a Toyota or a Honda or a Hyundai, you know, to a degree, that this vehicle is going to do the job,” he says.

“My two cents is that these vehicles are built to the same standards as pretty much anything else in terms of how sophisticated they are. But only time will unlock the truth or the falsity of that. The question we have is that, in a position where we are going to have 70 or 80 different brands from all over the world in this market, including 30-odd from China, can a market of our size truly support that in a sustainable, profitable, long-term way?

“The general sentiment in the industry is that it’s extremely difficult to imagine that we won’t see some brands pack up and leave because they just can’t sell enough vehicles to justify staying. Now, that may include some traditional brands, but it will also include some of these Chinese brands.”

It’s a thought echoed by Hyundai’s Romano, who suggests the collapse of brands in Australia – newcomer or legacy – could have a devastating ripple effect on customers and the market more broadly.

“The question is, are all of these brands going to survive? And I think the general consensus from every manufacturer is no. So the question then becomes, when they leave, who holds the warranty liability? I think it’s a worry that some of the big dealer groups are holding onto a number of brands that may or may not be around – and I’m not talking about Chinese brands, it could be any brand.”

The dominoes are wobbling. TrueEV, the Australian company responsible for selling and servicing models from the Chinese brand XPeng, had administrators appointed in March before closing its only Sydney showroom. XPeng’s Chinese HQ has since stepped in to establish operations in Australia and will set up its own dealer network for sales and servicing, in the same way brands like Toyota, Nissan or Mitsubishi are operated here. In July, the distributor for the French brand Peugeot relinquished its distribution rights for the brand, with the French marque’s future here currently uncertain, though it insists it will continue in some capacity.

The question, then, isn’t whether Chinese brands will succeed in reshaping Australia’s new-car market. Much like the BYD Zhengzhou, that ship has sailed. It’s which brands, household names or otherwise, will survive.

Exclusive Brethren secretly paid far-right activists to perform stunts disrupting the federal election

Sydney Morning Herald August 21, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Elders of a wealthy Christian sect secretly paid bundles of cash to far-right activists for an “influence campaign” to disrupt Albanese government appearances during the last federal election.

An investigation by this masthead has uncovered a digital trail of evidence revealing how the church, formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren, mobilised far-right figures around the country to track and heckle candidates from Labor and the Greens, along with independents, as part of a wider multimillion-dollar campaign for then-Liberal leader Peter Dutton.

When far-right influencer Laurence McIntyre yelled at Prime Minister Anthony Albanese about immigration on the first day of the election campaign, it looked like just a random attack from the fringes of politics.

But it was one of almost a dozen far-right stunts this masthead has traced back to the Brethren’s dirty tricks campaign. That includes – six political and church sources say – when the prime minister was twice ambushed in his hotel lobby by far-right figures boasting of being fed “private intel” on his location. The church categorically denies any involvement.

Leaked communications, insider accounts and social media footage now reveal the extent of the Brethren’s role in the 2025 election, as a spokesman for the sect, the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, prepares to give evidence on Friday to a parliamentary inquiry examining the scandal.

Four sources independently referred to a “duffel bag of cash” provided by senior Brethren members to a key right-wing figure who flew around the country helping coordinate the “influence campaign”.

The motley crew of agitators enlisted for stunts include McIntyre, who has links to neo-Nazis, as well as fringe politicians and pro-Putin conspiracists. The idea, according to five people with knowledge of the operation, was to disrupt the campaigns of Coalition opponents and push an anti-immigration message using already-notorious figures from outside the church. This would mask the Brethren’s involvement from the public – and from their own flock.

Senior Brethren elders used flight tracking apps to follow Albanese’s plane as it moved from city to city during the campaign, according to four sources who spoke anonymously due to safety concerns. At times, Brethren gophers lay in wait with far-right influencers to follow the prime minister’s car to hotels and events and even joined in the heckling of politicians.

This masthead has sighted internal communications confirming senior Brethren elders were involved in coordinating the stunts, including paying influencers. Thousands of dollars for the headline-grabbing antics changed hands. This masthead has seen evidence of payments behind many of the stunts and sources verify the rest, but has chosen not to name the church figures involved to protect those sources.

Some described cash being handed over in car parks and at “discreet meets” with Brethren or through intermediaries.

The stunts were filmed and splashed across right-wing media and social channels. Some were also posted by conservative lobby group Advance, which itself received $655,000 in political donations from Brethren businessmen last year. But Advance denied knowing who was involved or playing any role in Brethren campaigning.

4:21

The right-wing election stunts linked to members of a secretive church

An investigation by the Age tracked a mysterious slew of far-right stunts during the last federal election back to the Exclusive Brethren.

The Brethren church has itself consistently denied any involvement in the election, conceding that only its individual parishioners campaigned, not the church itself.

Asked about the right-wing agitators, a spokesman said: “If members did donate or have involvement with [any political party or third-party groups], that was under their name not the church’s.” He added that the church “completely rejects antisemitism”.

Key Brethren figures identified in the evidence and approached individually by this masthead denied they had planned, organised or funded the stunts. When asked about tracking Albanese’s plane, one elder said: “Anyone with a flight tracking app can do that.”

Two of the MPs on the committee now examining the Brethren’s conduct at the last election – Labor’s Jerome Laxale and independent Monique Ryan – were themselves targeted in the stunts.

Following the Coalition’s crushing election loss, sources within the church say elders and ordinary members have begun shifting their allegiance to Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. They warn that “the Brethren’s well-oiled influence machine” is not finished in politics yet, as an image surfaces showing a member campaigning for One Nation in Victoria last year.

Some within the sect say world leader, “Man of God” Bruce Hales, has signalled approval of One Nation’s policies, though that message has not appeared in his printed ministry. There is no evidence Hales was directly involved in organising or paying for the stunts.

Three church and political sources say senior Brethren members have trained in campaigning with Donald Trump’s MAGA movement in the United States. A Brethren business in Iowa hosted an election event in May featuring US Vice President JD Vance.

In early 2025, well before the May election, a few well-placed figures in the hard-right heard of a discreet opportunity. A group of “concerned Christian businessmen” were eager to stir things up on the campaign trail, to set the conditions for a Coalition victory – and they were willing to pay cash.

The Brethren seeking help from some of the “spicier” elements of the right all held influential positions within the church’s hierarchy. The sources say they were referred to as “the client” and often acted through the Brethren company Sante Global.

Between March and the May election day, about a dozen Brethren elders coordinated with far-right figures across the country, mostly using encrypted messaging apps, to pull off stunts targeting Albanese and Labor, as well as “teal” candidates and the Greens in Queensland, NSW and Victoria. At times, a small number of people connected to the Coalition were aware of the Brethren stunts, but sources say staffers didn’t appear to understand the full picture, and the party hierarchy was not involved.

As the effort was ramped up, this masthead has confirmed that a booking was made in the name of Sante Group at a Sydney golf club on April 1, 2025, bringing together state leaders from the Brethren, with a small clutch of their far-right helpers.

In the Brethren’s wider multimillion-dollar election effort for the Coalition, its members turned out to campaign undercover at polling booths in blue Liberal t-shirts despite their usual edict to shun the outside world. But now elders wanted to talk about more creative political strategies.

Among the far-right figures invited was vlogger Chris De Bruyne, who goes by Chriscoveries online. De Bruyne’s wife, Edwina Bull, endorsed posters during the campaign which were linked to the Brethren. These included the mysterious “Make Australia happy again” signs spotted on roadsides that April, reflecting a Brethren call to arms.

For weeks, De Bruyne had already been sharing and distributing many of the stunts in the Brethren operation. Some were carried out by his associates, one a pro-Putin agitator, and another: former Liberal Barclay McGain, who was fired from an MP’s office for posting racist comments in 2019 and now heads CPAC Australia.

Anti-lockdown “freedom party” founder Morgan C Jonas also shared and took part in some of the stunts. Posters he endorsed during the campaign were displayed by Brethren members – and flagged as non-compliant by the Australian Electoral Commission, which confirmed it is investigating wider concerns about Brethren involvement in 2025.

Jonas, who like De Bruyne has been linked to Advance campaigns, refused to answer questions, including about whether he was paid for taking part in the Brethren operation or endorsing their signage.

De Bruyne didn’t respond to requests for comment. The stunts are still prominently displayed on the website of the political lobbying firm he runs, Australian Firebrand, as an example of its recent “campaigns”.

The influence operation began even before the election, with Jonas targeting Foreign Minister Penny Wong as she attended a forum with the Chinese-Australian community in Box Hill in March 2025. The footage was shared by De Bruyne.

Next, ex-Liberal McGain crashed a Climate 200 event and yelled questions at teals donor Simon Holmes a Court – one of two stunts McGain carried out at candidate forums which were both disseminated online by De Bruyne.

McGain confirmed he’d passed footage of his stunts onto De Bruyne, though he denied being paid for them or knowing they were part of a coordinated campaign for the Brethren. Still, he said he wasn’t concerned they had been used in such an effort, as he thought it was “a good thing for more Christians to get involved in politics”.

On the first day of the election campaign, Albanese was targeted directly, when fringe influencer McIntyre heckled the prime minister at a Brisbane press conference. Among the close-knit stunt operators it was described as an “op”.

McIntyre, who uses the name “What’s News!?” online, later ambushed Greens MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown at a family picnic.

At the same time McIntyre was running Brethren stunts, he was also spruiking separate campaign hijinks online carried out by those he knew in the National Socialist Network, such as the neo-Nazi group’s fake flyer hoax spoofing Liberal party logos. There is no suggestion this stunt was funded by the Brethren.

Approached by this masthead, McIntyre said he had never heard of the Brethren, despite his inclusion in communications with church elders, but did not answer questions about whether he was paid. On the campaign trail, he was often joined in his stunts heckling politicians by another man, an “influencer” this masthead has identified as a long-time employee of a Brethren-owned company.

The stunts didn’t always go to plan. Sometimes agitators, and even Brethren members, were busted before they could sneak into candidate events. Once, multiple sources say, a car with Brethren gophers and far-right associates drew the brief notice of Albanese’s protective police detail while following the prime minister to an event in Queensland.

When the prime minister was ambushed – twice – in his Melbourne hotel lobby by two far-right figures, it raised security alarm bells.

At the time, one of the influencers involved bragged that he was part of a small, coordinated “team” given “private intel” on the prime minister’s location. But he would not say where it came from and did not answer questions this week.

Six political and church sources say both stunts were part of the Brethren’s efforts. “It felt like it was getting dangerous that they did those two,” said one. “But they were happy to let people assume it was the Nazis playing tricks again. If the rank-and-file Brethren found out they were using these grubby tactics, and these kind of people as guns-for-hire ... well, it hardly fits the Christian image.”

Watson-Brown said it had been clear that “there was big money and influence” at play during the campaign which “created a really quite sinister vibe”.

On the Coalition side, one source said with some electorates strapped for volunteers, it came down to each candidate’s team to either turn away or let in the “concerned Christians” offering help.

One Liberal MP refused Brethren help when members of the sect arrived at a polling booth in their campaign t-shirts. The next day, the MP recalled seeing the same people turn up in the shirts of the Liberal candidate from a neighbouring seat.

It’s unclear if the Liberal staffers made any connection between the Brethren donning campaign t-shirts and the far-right agitators crashing candidate events to film stunts.

“That was kept so tight to the chest,” one source said. “I don’t think even all of the far-right guys doing the stunts actually understood where the money came from, though some definitely did.”

Since Dutton’s loss at the ballot box, this masthead has been told very little has been said within the Brethren church about their failure to sway the result.

But various political sources say far-right figures and Brethren middlemen involved in the last election stunts have since reached out to smaller parties, including One Nation, to discuss how best to “help” going forward.

A Brethren member has been identified in photos from the last election campaigning for One Nation in Victoria. One Nation did not answer questions on whether they had had any dealings with the church.

In the days before the election, Brethren members were also told to turn out in force for an Advance “ute muster” against Albanese government policies for electric cars, according to internal Brethren communications.

Advance, which has been called to testify to the parliamentary inquiry on Friday into the 2025 election, said it “appreciated anyone who attended” its muster. But a spokesman said Advance had “never received money from a church” directly and “we do not screen our supporters based on their religion.”

Meanwhile, an AEC spokesperson confirmed the commission was now “examining the activities of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church and relevant entities and individuals to ascertain whether any entities or individuals had authorisation, registration and/or disclosure obligations under the Electoral Act”.

Electoral integrity expert Joo-Cheong Tham said there was “compelling evidence of a nationwide campaign coordinated by the organisational infrastructure of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church”.

He called revelations about “the covert funding and direction of far-right agitators by the Brethren” another way “in which the church seems to have concealed its large-scale election campaign”.

“It also raises more troubling questions. Why is the church supporting activities whose aim seems mainly one of electoral disruption? Does the church share the views of the agitators it supported?”

It posed a challenge to federal electoral laws and attempts to ensure transparency, Tham said, because the campaign involved coordinating volunteer labour and spending by a number of different entities.

One Coalition source said it was the deception that burned about the Brethren affair. “I don’t want these people hijacking my party!

“This isn’t MAGA America. This isn’t how we do politics.”

All those named in this story were contacted for comment.
