Reform’s new economic adviser has called for end of pensioners’ triple lock

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 17:36:17 GMT

Exclusive: Mitchell Palmer has also argued for privatising the NHS and immigration as way of cutting poverty

Reform UK’s new economic adviser has previously called the pensions triple lock unsustainable, advocated privatising the NHS and welcomed migration as a poverty alleviation tool, the Guardian can reveal.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s economic spokesperson, has appointed Mitchell Palmer, a rightwing economist at the free-market Adam Smith Institute, as one of his key aides.

Palmer’s background is as a champion of economic liberalism, in many cases putting him to the right of Reform’s existing policy platform. His appointment comes amid tensions within the party between those who want to lean into its tax-cutting agenda and those who worry that steep cuts to welfare and other government spending will alienate voters.

Palmer has previously called for the abolition of the triple lock, arguing it is an expensive and unsustainable way to protect pensioners.

He told GB News in April that he disagreed with Jenrick’s decision to back the triple lock, which guarantees that the state pension will rise by the highest of earnings, inflation and 2.5% every year. Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, had previously suggested the policy would be “up for debate”.

Palmer told the news channel: “The triple lock is an expensive way to ensure that pensioners have dignity in their retirement. There are ways that you can do that without the unpredictable ratcheting effect that the triple lock has.

“Pensioners almost by definition are made better off in real terms than workers and that obviously is, one, unsustainable as the number of pensioners that each worker has to pay for increases, but, two, can be seen by those younger generations as somewhat unfair.”

In a separate media appearance, this time on a podcast hosted by the former Conservative MP Steve Baker, he argued for the privatisation of the NHS. Asked by Baker if it was time to privatise the service, he replied: “Well it’s long past time, Steve.”

He went on to add: “The reality is the NHS is a horrifically performing system. It establishes much lower cancer survival rates. It has obvious rationing – we all know that when we try and get a GP appointment or a specialist appointment. It has a pretty bad safety record – that’s not for lack of spending.”

At times his commitment to liberal economics seems to go against Reform’s main policy positions. In 2020, when working in the New Zealand parliament, he argued online for the benefits of economic migration, posting: “Hot take: Allowing people in from abroad who choose to come to NZ and earn *significantly* more than they would at home is not slavery. In fact, it is one of the best contributions we can make to global poverty alleviation.”

Some of his other views include ending VAT exemptions and imposing a land tax.

A Reform spokesperson said: “Unlike the Guardian, Robert believes in hiring smart people with whom he disagrees.”

JD Sports boss is still struggling to turn up the heat on a tepid trainer market

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 17:14:31 GMT

Latest profit warning is particularly disappointing in a World Cup year, which should have given the global business a sporty buzz

JD Sports cuts £50m from profit forecast as cost of living pressures hit trainer sales

It was a slower quarter for “high-heat footwear product”, said JD Sports. It didn’t mean it was struggling to shift sandals during a heatwave. Rather, it was referring coyly to the big global trainer brands’ failure to come up with hot new designs. When Nike and Adidas, reckoned by City analysts to account for slightly more than half JD’s sales, are on tepid form, the self-styled “king of trainers” retailer usually is as well.

The low-heat grumble will be familiar to JD’s shareholders. So, too, the one about “incremental cost of living pressures”, especially in the US. And the phrase “a promotional market” has appeared so often in the company’s updates in the past couple of years that it would be easier to tell us when discounting isn’t dominant.

The result was another warning on profits and a 14% slump in the share price. JD now thinks it’ll make between £700m and £800m at an underlying pre-tax level this financial year. The difference from the previous estimate of £750m-£850m isn’t huge, but they all count. This was the third warning since early 2024. The particular disappointment this time is that it was a men’s football World Cup year, which ought to have been good for generating a general sporty buzz for a global business.

The market clearly is genuinely weak. Nike’s share price is down a third this year even after a miserable performance in the last two. Or look at Adidas’s own recent warning that its big marketing bet on the World Cup didn’t pay off. Or at the sluggish spending among US consumers in response to higher energy prices: Walmart, the largest US retailer, this week reported its slowest sales growth in six years.

Even so, the deeper worry at JD is that the whole “athleisure” trend isn’t coming back – or, if it does, at nothing like the level of the old days. The Covid pandemic created a mini-boom for joggers and trainers but since then the direction has only been one way. Did Nike and Adidas push prices too far? Have they been outflanked by the likes of Hoka and On? Or have consumer tastes just changed? Probably all of the above to an extent – and none is good news for JD.

The cashflow forecast, for £460m-£520m, didn’t change, which is evidence to support JD’s boasts about sharpening internal controls after its previous boom years of successful global expansion in the 2010s. All the same, waiting for an upturn, counting the cashflow and buying back a few shares makes for an uninspiring life.

Lack of water storage is an urgent national security issue

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 16:17:19 GMT

Readers respond to the crisis facing Britain caused by the lack of reservoir capacity and hotter summers

Your reporters came up with a good list of urgent climate policies in response to Andy Burnham’s somewhat surreal statement focusing on the sale of disposable barbecues following a Cobra meeting (From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now, 12 August), but they missed out the No 1 issue: the UK’s water-storage capacity.

It is blindingly obvious that we need to dramatically and rapidly increase water storage. The current plans to fast-track the building of nine reservoirs by 2050 might be speedy by the standards of UK infrastructure delivery projects, but they may well have been overtaken by climate change trends.

Indeed, if we had had forward-thinking governments and a functional water industry, some of them would have been built by now to match historic population growth. As it stands, only one reservoir is forecast to come online in the next 10 years.

Similarly, the building of farm-level water storage, which must be far simpler to deliver, appears mired in bureaucracy and is not rolling out nearly fast enough. Cutting through the red tape and supporting the building of thousands of farm ponds and small reservoirs would surely result in better crop yields while reducing pressure on summer water supply and wildlife habitat.

We urgently need to hear from the government on how it is going to address a national security issue that has moved from threat to living reality this summer. Simon DruryWandsworth, London

Your report on low reservoir levels (14 August) notes that no new reservoir has been built in the UK since 1992. Yet only months ago England emerged from its eighth wettest winter since records began, with rainfall 42% above the winter average. Now we are in drought.

The Victorians understood that reliable water supplies required storage. Faced with rapidly growing cities, they built reservoirs, aqueducts and local water-storage infrastructure. There are ageing water towers still dotted around Britain as monuments to the simple principle that it is sensible to store water close to where it will be needed. Governments like large infrastructure projects, and we undoubtedly need new strategic, large-capacity reservoirs. But these cost billions and can take many years to plan and build.

Why not also develop a national network of smaller modern distributed-storage reservoirs, either underground or covered, close to the communities they serve, capturing water during our wet winters? They would have the additional advantage of being installed incrementally rather than waiting years for huge projects to be completed. Pete Ford Sustainability lead, HealthTech Research Centre, Exeter

For the past 50 years we have lived in part of a large country house. We were lucky that a past owner was a forward-thinking architect who built a large underground tank to hold 20,000 gallons of rainwater gathered from the roof. He also installed a pump engine, now defunct, to bring water up 360 feet from an underground source to a reservoir, and we inherited a smaller underground tank not far from the vegetable garden.

With these three receptacles we have been able to store and pump water to our vegetable plots during the last two summers. Surely similar underground water storage could be incorporated into housing estates to take advantage of the wet spring seasons we have been having. Sheila Carey-ThomasAlton, Hampshire

We already are living with the reality of surge pricing for our water (Water companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during drought, 16 August). Anglian Water imposes a water tariff on Norwich that is around 2.5 times greater than the winter tariff. The outcome for two adults is a bill of £99.98 for 82 days between May and July 2026. We are low water users at 8 cubic metres, which is less than the typical usage for one person. We recycle water in the garden and apply the lessons of the summer of 1976 – except for sharing a bath, as we prefer showers. I can’t see what further reductions we can make. Maureen BegleyNorwich

The financial pressures described by university leaders (UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international students, 14 August) are both clear and serious, yet there are wider consequences of declining international student numbers that deserve attention.

While the immediate economic contribution that international students make is significant, so is their broader value in bringing international perspectives to our campuses, enriching the learning experience, and strengthening the UK’s relationships, reputation and influence around the world.

At a time when relationships, trust and influence increasingly matter, British Council research shows that studying in the UK can create enduring personal and professional connections. International graduates take those relationships into their careers, institutions and networks, maintaining connections with the UK long after their studies have ended, strengthening relationships, understanding and trust between the UK and countries around the world. UK universities are fundamental to that, and without them, this simply would not happen. Catriona McCarthyInterim director education, British Council

University leaders are right to warn of the financial turmoil in British higher education. Universities are undoubtedly facing uncertain futures. But those leaders must also shoulder some collective responsibility rather than reflexively laying blame elsewhere. It is a familiar refrain that when anything goes wrong the cause is external factors beyond the university’s control: first Covid, then energy prices and inflation, then frozen fees, and now the international visa system.

Any success, on the other hand, is claimed by university leaders as a sign of excellence. That excellence, however, is rarely managerial. Too many university leaders and senior managers have failed upwards from unexceptional academic careers to a gravy train of well-paid positions for which they lack the strategic foresight that would better serve their institutions.

This is the untold scandal of the higher education sector over the last decade. Did not one vice-chancellor understand that fees would not automatically increase with inflation after 2017 and put a plan in place to mitigate the effect on university finances? Did not the most basic analysis show that institutions were overreliant on international fee income?

The higher education workers at risk of redundancy are potentially losing their jobs not just because of external factors, but because of sector-wide mismanagement by university leaders too quick to shirk responsibility. Graham Thompson Emeritus professor of American literature, University of Nottingham

Why is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets?

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 16:14:59 GMT

As yields are dragged higher in the UK, Europe and Japan, the impact for consumers and businesses will be far-reaching

‘Starve the beast’? The $40tn cost of Republicans’ false promises to cut spending

Government borrowing costs around the world have surged to the highest levels in decades amid growing fears over US bond market turmoil.

Anxiety about Donald Trump’s handling of the US economy, and concern that the US president’s war with Iran is driving up inflation, are causing a sell-off in the US bond market.

Highlighting the world economy’s dependence on US stability, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on UK, French, German and Japanese government debt has been dragged higher.

Here we look at the factors driving the bond market, and the likely consequences.

Long-term US government borrowing costs have risen to the highest level since 2007, with the 30-year Treasury bond yield trading above 5%.

A bond is a form of loan that investors make to a borrower, or bond issuer. The yield represents the money an investor receives for owning the debt as a percentage of its current price. Prices fall when investor demand wobbles, which pushes up yields.

Against this backdrop, the US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said this week that Washington would at least double its purchases of long-term US bonds in an attempt to assuage investor concerns. Washington also staged a joint intervention this month with Tokyo to prop up the value of the Japanese yen.

Bessent’s intervention on Wednesday helped to push down yields, but the impact was only temporary: they were rising again on Thursday, reversing most of that early move.

With US Treasury bonds a lynchpin in global financial markets, the rise in US borrowing costs has dragged yields higher for other countries. G7 nations have faced among the sharpest increases: UK 10-year bond rates are close to the highest since 2008 and 30-year rates are near 1998 levels; Germany’s are at 2011 levels and France at a 16-year peak. Japanese borrowing costs have also hit the highest level since 1996.

The breakdown of negotiations in the US-Israel war on Iran is the main source of investor unease. The US national debt hitting $40tn (£29.3tn) for the first time – after having doubled over the past decade – is also stoking fear that Trump’s tax and spending plans are unsustainable.

The stop-start fighting in the Middle East has pumped up the oil price, adding to worries over inflation and the hit to economic growth worldwide.

Inflation is bad news for bond investors. This is because it undercuts the future value of money received for owning the debt, so investors demand a higher yield to compensate for the risk.

In response to the inflation shock, the world’s most powerful central banks are also increasingly expected to raise interest rates. However, the unpredictable nature of the Iran war, and of the Trump administration, are making the challenge tougher.

Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at Société Générale, said: “Many also believe US bonds are having a tantrum because new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, refuses to spoon-feed investors with the forward guidance they had become accustomed to.”

Investors are also worried by political risk: in the US, the fear is that Trump has little appetite to curtail soaring borrowing and debt levels. Investors have asked similar questions of Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, and France is preparing for an election year in 2027 amid mounting political schisms. Japan also faces challenges as it pumps up government spending despite elevated debt levels and with its currency under pressure.

Some analysts have also suggested Washington’s yen intervention was driven by worries about falling Japanese demand for US treasuries. Before the joint action, Tokyo had been attempting to prop up the currency by selling holdings of US treasuries to free up money to buy yen, which pushed down bond prices and lifted yields.

The AI boom is another factor. Silicon Valley companies are borrowing heavily to fund their rollout of datacentres, which means bond investors are being asked to swallow sizeable amounts of debt.

The impact is far-reaching. Higher yields will push up the costs for consumers and businesses for their mortgages, loans and corporate bonds – hitting their capacity to spend elsewhere, and weighing on the economy more broadly.

Governments worldwide, already awash with debt after the economic shocks of recent decades, are being squeezed. The rise in interest costs will not only add to Washington’s debt pile, complicating Trump’s tax and spending plans, but also make life harder elsewhere – including the UK and France ahead of tough budgets.

Some experts predict a doom loop whereby higher debt costs crowd out room for governments to spend on growth-enhancing measures, locking in weak economic growth and tax revenues and making budget deficits and rising debt levels more likely.

For the UK chancellor, John Healey, analysts at Société Générale expect the rise in borrowing costs could erase about half of the £23.6bn headroom left in reserve in the spring against the government’s self-imposed fiscal rules.

Much will depend on how the Iran war unfolds; and on whether the Trump administration changes course on tax and spending, or intervenes again in markets to support bond prices. The response from the world’s most powerful central banks will also be key.

The US has historically held an “exorbitant privilege” given the US dollar’s status as the global reserve currency, ensuring demand for dollar assets and enabling it to run persistently high trade and budget deficits. However, some analysts warn that the Trump administration is putting this at risk through the president’s trade policies and eye-wateringly expansive tax and spending plans.

The uncertainty comes as pressure is likely to mount on Trump in the run-up to the midterm elections in November.

Most investors will be looking for an easing in geopolitical tensions, further market intervention, or a shift in tax and spending policy from Washington. Central banks offering reassurance could also help.

However, some analysts warn that the ingredients are there for a market accident. Société Générale’s Edwards, who is famous for his gloomy predictions, said the conditions could be coming together for a US financial crisis.

Highlighting parallels to the conditions preceding the 2008 global stock market crash, started by the US sub-prime debt crisis, and the 1997 Asian financial crisis, Edwards said: “Just as well I have a long memory, for I can remember exactly what was happening in financial markets the last time French and US long bond yields were at these levels – c2007 and even further back to c1997 for Japanese and UK yields.”

Maracanã to host opening game and final at next year’s Women’s World Cup

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 15:25:54 GMT

Stadium has hosted two men’s World Cup finals

Arena Itaquera in São Paulo will host 10 matches

The Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro will host the opening game and the final of next year’s Women’s World Cup. The 78,838-capacity stadium, which hosted the finals of the 1950 and 2014 men’s World Cups as well as the finals of the Olympic football competitions in 2016, will be the venue for Brazil’s opening Group A match on 24 June, before staging the final on 25 July.

Fifa released the schedule for all 64 matches for the tournament, which features 32 teams. The draw will take place after more of the qualification playoffs have been contested.

Brazil will also play group matches at the Arena Itaquera in São Paulo – which will host 10 matches at the finals, more than any other host city – and at the Estádio Nacional in Brasília. Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo have been selected to host the semi‑finals, with the latter also staging the third-fourth playoff. All eight of the stadiums involved in the finals staged matches at the men’s tournament in 2014.

Belo Horizonte – the scene of Brazil’s humiliating 7-1 semi-final loss to Germany 12 years ago – has been chosen to host a quarter-final. The winners of Group A will play in that quarter-final if they progress that far. Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo will host the three other quarter-finals.

Porto Alegre and Recife are also staging matches in the 10th official edition of the Women’s World Cup and the second to include 32 teams, after the expanded tournament, cohosted by Australia and New Zealand, in 2023.

Spain won the title for the first time in Sydney after victory over England.

“We can’t wait to witness a new chapter of women’s football history unfold when the world’s best players, coaches, fans and local communities take centre stage in Brazil next year,” said Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino. “I already have goosebumps thinking about the incredible passion, colour and energy that Brazilian fans will bring to the tournament.”

Fat people cannot win, regardless of what we do. And I’ve had enough

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 15:00:54 GMT

Using weight loss drugs like Ozempic is not ‘cheating’ – and why does it matter how a person changes their body anyway?

As you might know if you read my columns, see me a mile away, or talk to me for five seconds, I am a card-carrying lifelong member of the Fat Lesbian Club. However, ever since I first laid eyes on the television show Roseanne (very important to me) as a small child, the actor John Goodman has held a special place in my heart. It was confusing for me: did I want to be Dan Conner, or be with Dan Conner? I’m still not sure. He has always been so hot to me, from Dan on Roseanne to Fred Flintstone to Walter in The Big Lebowski. His body has now drawn attention in the last week or so, after a photo of him showing significant weight loss went viral.

It’s not Goodman’s 74-year-old body (his choice) I want to discuss, but instead the arguments that broke out about how he lost the weight. On one side there were many people congratulating him on his hard work. Then there were people claiming he had taken Ozempic so it wasn’t actually hard work, and then there were people defending that by saying he’d been losing weight for years, so he’d done it the “right way”, actually.

I don’t know the details and I don’t care, but none of this is good. This is a common sentiment, but now it seems to be snowballing. There’s this idea that fat people who use weight loss drugs are “cheating” or “taking the easy way”. What it means, as usual, is that fat people cannot win, regardless of what we do. And I’ve had enough.

I’m a fat person. We are constantly badgered and tortured by a society that tells us to lose weight, at all costs. If you’re fat, that’s a moral failing: you’re lazy and unhealthy. If you’re fat at the gym, or jogging down the street, you’re an object of ridicule. If you lose weight with drugs, you didn’t earn it. If you’re fat and not self-flagellating at every moment, you’re glorifying obesity. If you lose weight for any reason, it then proves you were never really happy with yourself; it proves that fat is bad, that thinness was always the real goal. If you stay fat, we want you to admit you’re unhealthy. If you say you’re happy, we want to diagnose you with denial. So much of the condescension as well as plain cruelty towards fat people is packaged as “we just want you to be healthy”. If this were true (and if being skinny were the only marker of health, which it isn’t), nobody would be criticising John Goodman or other fat people for using medication, by saying it’s cheating.

“Cheating” implies you’re competing against someone. Who is being cheated if a fat person changes their body? What game are we playing? Why does it matter how a person changes their body – and why does any of it matter at all to non-fat people anyway? Just like basically every other human condition, there are a million reasons people’s bodies are different sizes and respond differently to different things. When someone quits smoking with medication, we don’t say they’ve cheated. We know that medication can be a tool. We don’t insist they go cold turkey to prove that they really wanted to quit. We understand in all other cases that making something easier, with less suffering, doesn’t make the outcome less legitimate. But when the body in question is fat, suddenly we become moral arbiters. Suddenly it matters how they do what we have savagely demanded they do.

Society has spent decades telling fat people that our value depends on our ability to control our weight. Now there is medicine that can make that control easier, and suddenly the problem is not the weight but whether the person has suffered sufficiently to “deserve” it. People resent us for being fat, and they resent us for getting thin. They just want us to suffer. All of this, as ever, is only about punishing fat people. People just hate us and our bodies, and they feel no shame about demonstrating that hatred, largely (no pun intended) because they are safe from being called out. It is perfectly socially acceptable to hate fat people.

This is not even about weight loss drugs – I don’t think everyone should take Ozempic, and I certainly worry about all the relatively thin people who seem to be taking it purely to get even thinner. I also don’t think being fat is inherently bad or good. I just think we should be treated like human beings. Is that really so much to ask? Apparently it is.

We should be allowed to lose weight without having to provide you with a moral explanation for how we did it. We should be allowed to remain fat without having to convince you that we are sufficiently miserable about it. We should be allowed to exercise, eat, dress, date, and just go about our lives without our bodies becoming public property. Fat people should not have to audition for your approval. We are human beings, our bodies are none of your business, and you need to keep your big fat noses out of our lives.

Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in Sydney

Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities minister

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 14:36:41 GMT

Exclusive: Bridget Phillipson says politicians have helped fuel hatred and that police are not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough

Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media.

Bridget Phillipson said she was increasingly worried about how commonplace misogyny and racism had become, fuelled by online interactions and statements by politicians she said would not have been acceptable a few years ago.

She accused senior MPs from Reform and the Conservatives of having made racist statements in recent years, and accused the police of not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough.

Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, she said: “I worry that we are at kind of a ground zero in terms of attitudes around violence against women and girls. Things that not very long ago felt totally unacceptable are becoming normal. I think we’re seeing that in terms of attitudes towards women, and I think we see that in terms of attitudes around racism.”

She accused the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, and Reform’s economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, of having made racist statements in recent years.

Earlier this year, Timothy called Muslims praying in Trafalgar Square an “act of domination”, while Jenrick came under fire in October after the Guardian revealed he had complained he “didn’t see another white face” on a trip to an area of Birmingham.

“We’ve had pretty despicable things that the likes of Robert Jenrick have said in the past on his visit to Birmingham,” she said. “We had Nick Timothy, who said some appalling things about Muslim prayer.

“Apparently I’m calling him names when I say that’s racist. I think it is fundamentally racist because I don’t think he would say that about any other group.”

Neither Reform nor the Conservatives responded to requests for comment.

Labour has been accused in recent years of shying away from criticising statements by Reform and Conservative MPs for fear of alienating their own voters. Phillipson’s comments suggest that under Andy Burnham ministers will be freer to take on their opponents more directly, even on sensitive issues such as race and gender equality.

Her comments about online misogyny underline the government’s determination to push through the under-16 social media ban, which was one of Keir Starmer’s last announcements in office and which ministers have promised will be in place by next spring.

The women and equalities minister also criticised the police for not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough. “We’ve seen some pretty shocking failings in terms of the police response over decades and sadly we’re not seeing the progress that we should in terms of how the police will often respond to this,” she said.

Labour itself is facing accusations of not taking violence against women seriously with its plan to release 5,000 prisoners earlyto free up space in crowded prisons.

Some in the party also think the government is veering into xenophobia with its proposals to toughen the immigration system and even deport children forcibly if their families refuse to move.

Phillipson defended the policies of the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, saying they were necessary to restore faith in the migration system. “Having public consent for migration and having a system that is fair is absolutely essential,” she said. “If you don’t have that, then everything falls away.”

Phillipson’s criticisms of other parties in part reflect her second role as party chair, which involves coordinating attack lines against Labour’s opposition. But it is also a sign of the personal animosity between her and senior Tory politicians, including the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch.

Badenoch has accused Phillipson, who raised taxes on private school fees as education secretary, of being a “spiteful class warrior”. The comments caused a row in the Commons chamber this year as the two MPs traded remarks.

Phillipson spoke in depth about that row for the first time since it happened, saying: “When she had her say, I just kind of said that people would find her out for who she really was.”

She added: “I’m from an ordinary working-class family in the north-east. They don’t like people like me making the argument for what I believe. For some of them, I guess they think I should just get back in my box.”

Having been moved by Burnham from her previous role, Phillipson said she was sad to leave her education brief, but said the new prime minister had lifted the mood within the party.

“There is a real sense of energy and hope and purpose,” she said. “My reflection on where we began in July 2024 is that a bit more of that would have probably got us a long way down the line.”

She added that Burnham had brought “a sense of hopefulness and optimism that I think people have felt has been lacking, not just actually since we came into government, but for years before that”.

She denied the party was planning to use the polling bounce it has seen since Burnham entered Downing Street to launch an early election. “We were elected with a five-year mandate in 2024, and I see no reason that we would depart from that,” she said.

‘I need to think like a CEO’: Weezer on the shifting sands of success, ugly feelings and the joy of spreadsheets

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 14:16:19 GMT

As the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativity

The first song Rivers Cuomo wrote for Weezer’s new album, their 20th, blatantly mimics the US rockers’ 1994 debut single, Undone (The Sweater Song). On the track CEO, the singer-guitarist grumbles over a slow, Velvets-y backing about having to crank out “another 90s jam” and wishing he could do “something new – but nobody wants to hear that”. It’s a deliciously meta moment, but also one that allows Cuomo to gently vent “my frustrations over people wanting me to just write songs about our first two albums”.

Cuomo wrote the song straight after SZNZ, the four-album song-cycle Weezer released throughout 2022, each album named after a season. That project fed his notoriously intense, analytic and occasionally obsessive approach to songwriting. Thanks to the kind of data artists have at their fingertips in the streaming age, though, he realised that, with each subsequent SZNZ, “fewer and fewer people were listening to them”.

His response was to “think strategically”. On a video call from his home in Santa Monica, California, where Cuomo, 56, lives with his wife and children, he says he realised: “If I want people to listen to my music, I need to think less like a mad scientist in the research and development department and more like a CEO.” Accordingly, he took several years off from releasing any new material (“to build up demand”), ditched the high concepts of SZNZ and focused on creating what he thinks the fans want.

Like six previous albums, the new album is titled Weezer. It has already been dubbed the “gold” album by fans, due to its sleeve colour. While the arch lyrics to CEO might suggest it is a cynical exercise in pandering to his audience, the Gold Album is a more complex, sophisticated beast.

Cuomo is driven by his obsession with songwriting. “It’s like building sonic architecture, such a cool, stimulating experience,” he says, although he prefers to describe himself as a “composer”. “The term ‘songwriter’ feels like Paul Simon’s about to explain a sombre part of life,” adds his bandmate Patrick Wilson, 57, who plays drums and guitar and joins the interview from the garage of his California home. “What we do is more visceral: busting out a sick riff and saying to each other: ‘Dude, check this out!’”

Cuomo’s approach is methodical to a degree that feels antithetical to rock music; he has boasted that Google Sheets is integral to his process. (One spreadsheet, which he has named “The Encyclopedia o’ Riffs”, keeps track of all his unused and unfinished ideas and is legendary among Weezer fans.) He also can’t resist a kooky conceptual hook to guide his songwriting – see the group’s 2021 heavy metal set, Van Weezer, or OK Human, their orchestral rock opus of the same year, or, obviously, SZNZ.

The Gold Album is similarly conceptual, this time the concept being the creation of an album the Weezer faithful will love. Cuomo’s process has been typically analytical and methodical – and it’s clear he has loved the challenge. He views their live shows as the testing ground for the new material – “where the rubber meets the road”, he says. “I want the people in the room to want to hear these new songs as well as our old hits, and to sing along. I wanted them to be really fun live, to have substantial riffs and guitar parts.” Accordingly, he has taken inspiration from his favourite band of the moment, the Swedish heavy rockers Ghost, whom he says restored his understanding of “the power of stadium-rock riffage”. Nevertheless, much of the Gold Album channels the loud guitars and pop-oriented tuneage of Weezer’s eponymous 1994 debut, often brilliantly so.

The new album is shaped by deeper wounds than those occasioned by SZNZ’s reception, however. The line in CEO where Cuomo says he has “gotta keep this rocket in the sky” references the moment when the failure of Weezer’s second album, 1996’s Pinkerton, seemed to hobble their career before it began – a foundational trauma for the group’s leader.

He remains the pilot of his bandmates’ fortunes as much as his own and, while the Gold Album sounds bold and confident, there are moments in our interview when his anxiety over this responsibility surfaces. They collaborated more as a group on the songwriting of the Gold Album than any previous Weezer release; while Cuomo talks about how their positive feedback was “a real good sign” he might be on the right track with an idea, it’s clear he chiefly prized their solidarity as a group “to give us the strength to face any pushback from the audience”.

Raised in a Buddhist ashram in Connecticut, which taught him methods to “calm down my body and mind”, Cuomo became a teenage metalhead and, in his late teens, under the influence of the Swedish poodle-rocker Yngwie Malmsteen, formed the hair-metal group Avant Garde. That group renamed itself Zoom and relocated to Los Angeles to make it big, but within a year they had imploded and Cuomo began working at Tower Records in West Hollywood.

This disappointment – alluded to on The LA Sound, a song from the Gold Album, written by guitarist Brian Bell, about a no-hoper metal band running aground on the Sunset Strip circuit – was “heartbreaking”, says Cuomo. But it proved the making of him. “If Zoom had ‘happened’, if my dreams had come true, I would just be the lead guitar player – the second lead guitar player, excuse me – in a heavy metal band that would have been woefully out of style by 1992. Instead, my heart got broken and that led to something a lot bigger and better: singing, and expressing myself, and focusing on songs rather than shredding.”

Weezer formed shortly after Nirvana’s fateful breakthrough. Cuomo had been seduced by the Pixies’ “big crunchy guitars, melody and heaviness” – one of numerous artists he discovered through his Tower co-workers. On Weezer’s earliest demos, he “tried singing like Black Francis or Kurt Cobain or Perry Farrell, more of a ‘rock’ voice. It took months before I finally gave up and sang with my natural, pure voice. I’d sung in school choirs; to my surprise, it still worked, even over the big guitars.”

It wasn’t just Cuomo’s voice that set Weezer against the grain. They wore glasses and unhip clothes, while Cuomo sang about comic books and Dungeons & Dragons. The rock press identified them as nerds, a label they never quite shook loose and ended up embracing: they kicked off this year’s Weezer: The Gathering tour, named after the fantasy card game Magic: The Gathering, with a pickleball tournament with their fans. Regarding this resistance to cool, Cuomo says they “just felt it was very uncool to try and be something you’re not”.

“The kids today would call it ‘being a sweat’,” says Wilson, un-coolly. “In hip-hop, they would have called it ‘fronting’.”

This honesty – along with Cuomo’s infallible gift for pop songcraft – struck a chord in the post-Nirvana cash grab. But as their debut began its ascent to quintuple-platinum status, via a punishing schedule of touring and promotion, Cuomo’s morale plummeted. In his diaries, he wrote of his dissatisfaction with this new rock’n’roll life. Addressing an imaginary rock-star-in-waiting, he gloomily advised: “You will get lonely … It’s not all cocaine, chicks and limos.”

His face is mostly obscured by shadow on our call, but Cuomo’s disillusionment remains palpable three decades on. “All my life. I’d figured that if I got a record deal – if we got on MTV and radio – then I would feel fulfilled and loved,” he says. “We achieved all those things. But I still felt unseen and unheard and misunderstood and lonely.”

Cuomo abruptly ditched the tour bus for Harvard, where he studied classical composition alongside students sporting Weezer T-shirts, oblivious to his presence. The course deepened his feel for songwriting. “Creatively, I was feeling incredibly confident. I was not happy about my personal life, but believed if I isolated myself – and, to an extent, tortured myself – I would be able to create something really great.” He pauses. “I was probably overconfident.”

Inspired by the antihero in Puccini’s Madama Butterfly, he wrote Pinkerton, an ambitious, strikingly unguarded confession that success had left Cuomo engulfed by loneliness, disaffection and sexual confusion. Before the album’s 1996 release, he warned the Weezer fanclub that it included “all the parts of myself that I was either afraid or embarrassed to think about before. So there’s some pretty nasty stuff on there.”

Sure enough, Across the Sea depicts him falling in love with a Japanese teenager who wrote him a fan letter (“I wonder what clothes you wear to school … I wonder how you touch yourself”); on Pink Triangle, he grumbles about a lesbian who doesn’t fancy him; and, on The Good Life, he’s “a pig, I’m a dog, so ’scuse me if I drool”.

The album was, he says, an act of catharsis. “It’s always been hard for me to communicate feelings in words, in conversation,” he sighs. “But if I can play them through melodies and chords and lyrics, I feel this tremendous emotional release.”

It was all done with lashings of self-mockery and knowing awfulness, but plenty of fans recoiled. Even Ric Ocasek, the producer of their debut, didn’t seem to like it. Pinkerton flopped; Cuomo put Weezer on hiatus and went into hiding. It was “a chaotic era”, says Wilson, who worried about the impact of Weezer’s steep arc on Cuomo. “I wondered how child stars dealt with success. And I realised: they’re all insane, because it’s a ridiculous process. That period was overwhelming.”

“I’d keep feeling like I’d found my way out, that the way back was just around the corner,” Cuomo remembers, of the struggle to write a third Weezer album. “But each time, just as I’d be about to announce to the guys I had songs I felt confident in, my confidence would collapse again: these songs are terrible. Let me start over. Give me a few months.”

Salvation came in 2000, in the form of an unexpected six-figure offer to play Japan. After four years of darkness and frustration, Cuomo remembers being “in tears” when his manager called with the news. Next, the band jumped aboard that summer’s Warped tour and discovered that, in their absence, Pinkerton had found an audience that treasured its confessional intensity. “Our fans were out of their minds, chanting: ‘Weezer! Weezer!’ all through the bands on before us,” remembers Wilson. “I knew something was up. Like: oh. We’re going to be OK.”

Today, Pinkerton is recognised as a pivotal emo album. Its follow-up – 2001’s Green Album, again produced by Ocasek and containing the single Hash Pipe – was a platinum-selling hit. “I remember thinking: if we can survive the last five years of solitude and self-doubt and come back to this, we can get through anything,” Cuomo says. “Our fans pulled us out of our self-doubt.” Today, those fans log in to Cuomo’s personal Discord server and watch him practice vocal warm-ups or play Beethoven on his piano. “There’s always this group of people online that love me and appreciate me and are looking forward to hearing anything I’m doing, so I never have to feel alone,” he says.

The fans have stayed loyal as Cuomo has explored unexpected directions – such as the heavy metal of Van Weezer and the orchestral rock of OK Human – and collaborated with songwriters outside his realm, including Linda Perry, Jermaine Dupri and Justin Hawkins of the Darkness. He confesses his obsession with songwriting isn’t always healthy: “There were times where my wife was going through troubles and she really could have used my help. And I would spend all day in my room, just working – super-deep, detailed work – and I told her, like: ‘I can’t help you right now, I’m on a roll here, I really need to focus.’ There has been some conflict.”

This hasn’t happened recently, though, he says. Three decades after the existential wobble of Pinkerton, Cuomo seems happy keeping Weezer’s rocket in the sky. He feels lucky to “have this vocation with these three other guys. We can get in a room together and work on stuff that feels important to us. As you get older, it can be hard to have those kinds of relationships. But we have them.”

The relationships have held strong through traumas that might have destabilised other groups, such as the 2011 death of bassist Mikey Welsh from a suspected drug overdose. The bandmates all “get along pretty great now”, says Wilson. “We all have perspective on everything now. We see how everything unfolded and how deeply unusual it was, and we recognise it.”

Can Cuomo see a time in his life when Weezer isn’t a thing? On the sleeve to 2005’s Make Believe – released during a period of emotional anxiety and voluntary celibacy, for spiritual reasons – he included the soliloquy from The Tempest, where Prospero abandons his magic and commits to “drown my book”.

“At the time, I wasn’t sure I was gonna go on making music,” Cuomo says. “I wanted to try a really intense spiritual path and then start a family. I wanted to step away from the spotlight, from being an artist, even from being creative, and see what else there is in life. So I included that speech, like: OK, maybe this is my retirement statement.” He stops. For one of the few times during our chat, he looks up from the shadows and into his laptop camera, smiling. “But it’s obvious, isn’t it? Come on, Rivers. You can’t escape this.”

Weezer is released via Reprise/Warner on 21 August

The best hair oils for glossy, healthy looking locks

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 14:00:53 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

They’re all the rage, but which scalp serums, oils and capsules can be counted on for nourishment and serious shine?

The best hair masks for every budget, tested

Hair oil has become increasingly popular, with countless celebrities and influencers lauding its ability to smooth, protect and support hair growth. Some apply hair oil to their scalp, others to their strands; some apply oil to wet hair before styling, others use it on a finished style. With so many uses, it’s worth thinking about your goals before buying.

I’ve worked my way through 11 bottles, from a cheap-and-cheerful £9.99 to a steeper £65, to bring you this list of the best hair oils. Whether you’re looking for thick, nourishing oils to help nurse damaged hair to life or a featherlight option to add shine and scent to your strands, there’s something on this list for you.

Besides testing on my own locks, I spoke with trichologist Hannah Gaboardi to find out if and how hair oils can actually support hair growth. Read on for her comments and my nine favourite hair oils.

Best hair oil overallGisou Honey infused hair oil, 50ml

Best budget hair oilHask Repair Series hair oil mist, 120ml

Best hair oil for damaged hairK18 Molecular Repair hair oil, 30ml

Best lightweight hair oilGoldwell Smooth Weightless Shine oil, 100ml

Best smoothing hair oilArkive The Good Habit hybrid oil, 50ml

Hair oils have been a staple of my hair care routine for the past few years. I’ve tried thicker oils that weigh hair down, and thinner oils that barely touch the sides of my dry ends. My hair has always been long, and for most of this testing process, I had waist-length hair that hadn’t been cut for a year. If an oil could nurse my ratty old ends back to health, it was a winner.

I’m also a beauty journalist, so I spend my life learning about advancements in hair care, from keratin bond fixers that “repair” hair strands to scalp-soothing formulas that support hair growth. A cosmetic science course has given me a background knowledge of all things hair health, from the scalp, right down to the cellular structure of hair.

I tested 11 hair oils from the most popular brands, noting how each product affected the finish of my hair, mainly focusing on how hydrated it felt. As part of the testing process, I also assessed the consistency and greasiness of each one. If it was scented, I also checked to see how well the scent lingered on my hair.

In terms of ingredients, I looked for nutrients and vitamins that help to seal the cuticle and protect each strand from environmental stress. As always, price was a factor: you can forgive a lot more from a cheap hair oil than an expensive one.

Gisou’s honey-infused hair oil has been my go-to for more than a year now. Its thicker texture is perfect for nourishing the dry ends of my hair, adding a dose of hydration and shine where it needs it most.

Why we love itGisou is known for its honey-powered hair care, and the hair oil is a hero product. The Mirsalehi honey included in this formula is rich in protective antioxidants and minerals, but also has humectant properties to hydrate each hair strand. It also works beautifully alongside the emollient coconut and sweet almond oils in the formula to smooth out hair.

In my experience, a small amount of this hair oil goes a long way. I found it easy to disperse through my long hair after warming it in my hands and loved the glossy shine it gave, while making my hair strands feel stronger and preventing breakage. As with all the Gisou honey products, it also smells divine.

It’s a shame that … its slightly thicker texture won’t be for everyone. If you don’t have issues with dryness or have very fine hair that can’t handle richer products, opt for something else.

Size: 50mlPrice per ml: 74pKey ingredients: Mirsalehi honey, coconut oil, sweet almond oilVegan? NoCertified cruelty-free? NoSuitable for: wet and dry hair

If you want to avoid greasy hands, this lightweight hair oil mist from Hask is ideal. Simply spritz over your hair to evenly disperse a fine layer of oil, leaving smooth, shiny and lightly scented locks. It shone in my tests, despite its low cost, demonstrating brilliant value for money.

Why we love itOther than its bargain price and clean application, I found this oil added shine without weighing my hair down or making it feel greasy. Its atomiser consistently produced a fine mist, giving a lovely, even coating of fresh floral-scented oil on my locks.

The spray contains hydrating argan oil, as well as Hask’s trademarked RepairPro, which it claims can “repair” bleach-damaged hair by up to 98%. I couldn’t test this claim at home, but I can attest that my hair felt noticeably smoother after use. The silicones in the formula help to seal and smooth the hair cuticle, preventing snagging and further damage.

It’s a shame that … these silicones can build up over time if they aren’t washed off correctly, or if they’re overused, which leads to more brittle hair in the long term.

Size: 120mlPrice per ml: from about 8pKey ingredients: argan oil, RepairProVegan? YesCertified cruelty-free? YesSuitable for: wet and dry hair

If you’re looking to include hair oil in your routine, chances are you’re hoping to counteract the signs of damaged hair – dryness, frizz and dullness. While no hair product can fuse split ends back together, the “molecular repair” element of this hair oil refers to an increase in hair strength and elasticity observed on bleach-damaged hair strands in the brand’s testing. After use, bleach-damaged hair should be less prone to breakage and more resilient to daily stressors, such as brushing, sun exposure and heat styling. This is easily the hardest-working hair oil you can buy, justifying its high cost – and it’s my favourite oil on test if you don’t take price into consideration.

Why we love itThis hair oil works to help hair strands look and feel stronger using K18’s patented peptides. The formula mimics the natural peptides that give healthy hair its structural integrity, which are diminished when hair is bleached, dyed or styled with heat. Packed in, you’ll also find antioxidant avocado and sunflower oils to condition the hair. Meanwhile, squalane and hemisqualane soften the hair and smooth the cuticle, locking in that goodness without the need for heavy silicones.

This oil can be used either on damp hair before heat styling or as a finishing flourish to add shine to styled hair. Thankfully, and perhaps counterintuitively when applying an oil to your hair, it offers heat protection up to 232C – so you don’t have to worry about it frying your locks. It’s a concentrated oil, giving a lightweight, even coating, and just a few drops left my locks looking instantly shiny and healthy.

It’s a shame that … it’s expensive. If you already have healthy-looking hair, you really don’t need to spend this much.

Size: 30mlPrice per ml: about £2.17Key ingredients: squalane, avocado oil, sunflower oil, sh-Oligopeptide-78Vegan? yesCertified cruelty-free? YesSuitable for: wet and dry hair

Even the best hair oils can be too thick and goopy for some people, especially those with fine locks and oily scalps. This lightweight and affordable oil from Goldwell is perfect for adding a touch of glossy shine without weighing down the hair.

Why we love itThis oil has an incredibly thin texture that feels completely weightless when applied. I used it to top off a bouncy blow-dry and it added a lovely shine while keeping the movement and volume I wanted. I was also impressed by how it handled frizz – Goldwell claims it can tame frizz for up to 72 hours, and I can confirm my hair stayed silky smooth on a particularly humid day in central London.

Inside the formula, you’ll find Himanthalia elongata extract (or sea spaghetti), which helps to moisturise hair. This is another oil that can be used on damp or dry hair, and I loved its uplifting, sweet, fruity scent. I simply rubbed any left over into my skin after use, and it didn’t leave my hands feeling sticky or greasy.

It’s a shame that … like many hair oils, it uses dimethicone, a silicone that could build up on the hair if overused and not cleaned out properly. It also doesn’t have as many oils blended in as other options, so it doesn’t feel quite as nourishing as heavier, oilier formulas.

Size: 100mlPrice per ml: 17pKey ingredients: dimethicone, isoamyl laurate, Himanthalia elongata extractVegan? YesCertified cruelty-free? YesSuitable for: wet and dry hair

If you have thick, frizzy hair that takes a lot of taming, this affordable hair serum-oil hybrid could be the fix you need. Simply add a pump or two to damp, clean hair after washing and conditioning, style your hair as usual and watch it work its magic.

Why we love it This hybrid oil contains baobab and jojoba oils, which add shine and moisture to the hair. Jojoba oil is also an emollient that forms a protective layer to lock in the hair’s moisture and to give super sleek, smooth results. Used before styling, the oil helps protect your hair from heated tools, creating a shiny finish that was humidity-proof in my tests.

I loved this oil’s delicate scent, with slightly fruity top notes, a light floral heart and a musky vanilla base. I was also pleased to learn that this fragrance stuck around after application.

The next thing I noticed was its very thick, gel-like consistency. Even after warming the oil in my hands, it had a sumptuous, thick texture that properly coated each strand. This coated feeling vanished as soon as I styled my hair using a hot brush, leaving my strands looking hydrated, healthy and frizz-free.

It’s a shame that … it uses the silicone dimethiconol to smooth the hair, which is effective at smoothing and preventing frizz, but can cause buildup when not washed out properly.

Size: 50mlPrice per ml: 27pKey ingredients: baobab oil, jojoba oil, dimethiconol Vegan? YesCertified cruelty-free? YesSuitable for: wet and dry hair

Best for: natural ingredients and heat protection

You’ve no doubt heard of Dyson’s hair dryers and stylers, but fewer people know about the brand’s recent expansion into hair care. Among Dyson Beauty’s latest launches is the Omega hydrating hair oil, which uses sunflower seed oil grown on Dyson farms to hydrate and nourish hair.

More specifically, the Omega oil combines seven oils, each rich in omega fatty acids. These are sunflower, macadamia, avocado, olive, abyssinian, sesame and corn, and they work together to boost moisture, reduce frizz and protect hair against breakage. The Dyson hair oil also provides heat protection up to 230C, so you can style without damage.

In my tests, I loved how lightweight this oil was and enjoyed its uplifting, subtle fragrance. I found it easy and comfortable to apply to my strands, and my dry ends felt far healthier after application. Its smoothing performance was middling, but this was a compromise I was willing to accept, considering the formula is free from silicones.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s expensive and its lid likes to slowly open itself over time. I certainly wouldn’t want to store this hair oil lying down. Luckily, it looks lovely and sculptural on a vanity table.

Size: 30ml; price per ml: from about £1.53; key ingredients: sunflower oil, macadamia oil, avocado oil, olive oil, abyssinian oil, sesame oil and corn oil; vegan? Yes; certified cruelty-free? No; suitable for: wet and dry hair

Best for: fine hair

This lightweight hair oil smooths frizz using a blend of argan, sunflower seed and camellia seed oils. It’s the perfect consistency for fine hair, for which thicker oils are too heavy. It absorbed quickly, without leaving an over-greasy feeling on my hands. Once applied, I noticed my hair had a lovely shine to it and felt smooth and well-conditioned, with frizz and flyaways staying away even in high humidity.

The brand claims that this hair oil helps protect against UV-induced colour fading, so it could be a good option for those with dyed hair. And, if you travel often, the small lightweight bottle is far more secure than others I’ve tested.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s too lightweight to benefit those with very thick, dense hair. Its pouring dispenser is also difficult to control.

Size: 50ml; price per ml: 68p; key ingredients: argan oil, sunflower seed oil, camellia seed oil; vegan? Yes; certified cruelty-free? Yes; suitable for: wet and dry hair

Best for: scalp care and supporting hair growth

Put down the rosemary oil. To best support hair growth, you want something water-based that can quickly and weightlessly penetrate the scalp, not just sit on top of it and cause buildup, like an oil. This lightweight, water-based serum from Ireland-based scalp-care brand Remi is what you need.

This serum is formulated with rosemary extract and vitamin E. Both of these are antioxidants that help calm the scalp and protect it from environmental stress, while the multitasking rosemary extract helps promote microcirculation. This helps to keep the scalp feeling healthy and calm while the microcirculation increases blood flow, which feeds the hair follicle, creating the perfect environment for healthy hair growth. Hair loss can be caused by multiple factors, from hormones to genetics, so no hair oil or serum will fix that. However, hair grows best from a healthy scalp, so it makes sense to take care of it.

In my tests, I was amazed by how lightweight this serum was. With a quick massage, my scalp instantly drank it up and was left feeling just as clean as when I started. I could apply this four or five times before it started to weigh down my hair.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not exactly a hair oil. But if you want to apply something to your scalp that will support its health and, in turn, support hair density, pick this lightweight serum instead.

Size: 100ml; price per ml: 47p; key ingredients: rosemary extract, glycerine, vitamin E, peptides; vegan? Yes; certified cruelty-free? No; suitable for: damp and dry scalp

Best for: intense treatment

This hair oil is incredibly rich and covers everything your hair needs to thrive. It includes omega fatty acid-rich Moroccan oil to add shine, while jojoba oil helps reduce breakage. You’ll also find moisturising vitamins A, C and E and moisture-locking vitamin B5. This oil smoothed my hair and enhanced shine, and, despite its thicker texture, didn’t weigh it down.

The oil comes encased in capsules, each containing one application. It’s intended to be used as an intensive treatment weekly after washing and before styling, which means you only need to get your hands oily once a week, rather than daily. I thought the biodegradable capsules stank a bit, but the oil itself smells nice and fresh once out of the capsule.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found the hair oil capsules tricky to open without scissors, and messy to use when I eventually managed it.

Size: 30ml; price per ml: from about 58p; key ingredients: Moroccan oil, jojoba oil, aloe vera oil, vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin E; vegan? Yes; certified cruelty-free? No; suitable for: wet and dry hair

“Hair oils are a more natural way of moisturising the hair shaft,” says trichologist Hannah Gaboardi. “They penetrate into the cuticles and provide them with the vitamins, nutrients and fatty acids needed for healthier hair.” Hair oils can add moisture to support dry, brittle hair, she adds, and when applied regularly, they can add shine and tame frizz.

Some people apply hair oil to their scalp. This “can help promote hair growth by improving the circulation”, Gaboardi says. “More blood flow to the scalp allows the follicles to receive more nutrients.” Just always make sure you cleanse your scalp thoroughly afterwards to prevent clogging.

Not exactly. Hair growth rate is determined by many factors, including age, hormones and scalp health. Hair oils can only help with scalp health, and they need to be used correctly to make a big difference.

“Hair oil won’t directly grow your hair, especially when your hair loss is caused by genetic factors or health conditions,” says Gaboardi. The good news is that the nutrients, vitamins and fatty acids that make for healthier hair also benefit the hair follicles. “Hair oil also helps moisturise the scalp to create a healthy environment,” she says.

But it’s not all sunshine and roses. “When hair oil is used incorrectly, it can damage scalp health and can clog the pores in your scalp,” Gaboardi cautions. “This can cause a delay in the natural hair cycle and slow down growth if [the oils are] not washed out. It can also lead to sebum buildup and cause seborrheic dermatitis.”

This question has confused me for years. Some hair oils are designed to be used on freshly washed, damp hair before styling. Others are better suited to adding shine to finished styles. But surely adding a hair oil before using heat styling tools is a recipe for disaster that can only result in damaged locks?

The answer to my fears lies in an oil’s smoke point. Smoke point is the temperature at which oils begin to smoke and break down. “Oils that have a lower smoke point can cause the hair further heat damage when combined with high heat tools,” says Gaboardi.

Avoid using hair oils containing oils with a smoke point of below 177C, such as flaxseed oil or extra virgin olive oil, before heat styling. Luckily, few hair oils contain these.

Instead, “oils that have a high smoke point can be used after hair washing to help retain moisture and defend against heat”, says Gaboardi. These include grapeseed oil, safflower seed oil, argan oil and avocado oil. If you’re in doubt, she recommends “using serums and oils designed for heat styling to ensure you’re safely treating your hair”.

“Certain oil types have antioxidant properties that are used as a shield against UV rays,” says Gaboardi. At the same time, some oils provide natural, albeit low, protection against UV rays.

If you notice your hair getting drier and frizzier when exposed to the sun, using a hair oil can help keep your hair smooth and nourished. That’s because hair oil helps lock moisture into the hair strand that could otherwise dry out in the heat.

Sarah Matthews is a health and beauty consumer journalist who’s tested everything from hi-tech skincare gadgets to hair styling tools. With four years of hands-on experience, she’s built a reputation for honest, detailed reviews across hair removal, light therapy, and more. As someone with waist-length hair, she’s developed strong opinions on everything from heat protection sprays to detangling brushes

Amy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 13:00:52 GMT

As her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tour

You wrote Bring Me to Life when you were 19. When you perform it now, how do you relate to the younger you? becgoldsmithI was in an abusive relationship, so Bring Me to Life was partly about processing the reality of that abuse and asking myself, what are you gonna do about it? Like, pick yourself up. I wrote it when I was crushing on my [now] husband, but the theme is about a quest for something bigger: opening your heart, finding more depth. It’s very empowering to perform it now in huge places; I’m very proud of the 19-year-old me that wrote it.

Artists often reveal their influences through the songs they choose to cover. You’ve performed both It’s a Fire and Glory Box by Portishead. What drew you to those songs? VerulamiumParkRangerBeth Gibbons was one of my greatest vocal and musical inspirations. In the 90s when I was a young teen really feeling music I loved Portishead, Massive Attack and the whole trip-hop vibe. It was dark and cool, really different. Beth’s vocals have a way of teetering on an emotional crack, on the edge of wild, barely restrained emotion but never belting, which I always thought was so cool and enticing. I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers.

Your new album, Sanctuary, feels delicately balanced between healing and reflection, but also anger about what is going on in the world right now. How did you manage that balance and how do you feel about using your voice to stand up against what’s wrong? Amlou7 I hate politics, but our existence is political. Most of us don’t want anything to do with the atrocities that are going on today, but as human beings with hearts and souls we must rise to the occasion. I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet or making me feel uncomfortable speaking about what we’re now calling politics, which is life and death, rape, genocide, stealing from people. Music has always been an outlet for whatever’s in my heart, so now the music is an outlet for those big things. I meet so many people around the world with different beliefs, and we’re not that different. Most people are good human beings who would help you if you were injured, and that goodness is precious and worth fighting for. We have to be strong and keep calling things out and not back down to fascism.

Can you share any funny stories of things that have happened during the current Sanctuary tour? Andrew_ClevelandThere’s so many, we could make a blooper reel of all the mistakes. When you put yourself out there with a big production inevitably there’s more potential for things to go wrong. We have a moment where a kabuki [Japanese theatre] curtain drops down dramatically behind me. It’s beautiful, but in windy amphitheatres there’s been a couple of funny moments where it’s come down in the wrong place and dropped right on my head. It’s been great touring with Spiritbox and Nova Twins and we do a song together, Fight Like a Girl. One night, I sang entirely the wrong thing. Spinal Tap is totally like reality. I’ve experienced that scene of walking round in circles not being able to find the stage more times than I can count.

What are your thoughts on Nathan Fielder’s use of Bring Me to Life in The Rehearsal season two [he speculates that Captain Chesley ‘Sully’ Sullenberger listened to the song before successfully landing a passenger plane on the Hudson River]? thunderponceIt’s amazing to me that the song has reached so far, but that was just one of those surreal moments where you really think, “Wow, this is wild.” I thought it was strange and brilliant, like Nathan Fielder is. I had tears in my eyes by the end. It was so beautiful. I’m not saying Bring Me to Life helped land the plane, but it’s a cool way to demonstrate how music inspires people in stressful or big moments. Bring Me to Life has been used in all sorts of things and it took me a long time to get past the cynicism of “I don’t know about this … ” but I feel safe in it now.

I recently lost my 14-year-old dog and five-year-old cat, and listening to the Secret Door has been one of the only things helping me lately. The lyrics are beautiful and eerie, the background melodies reminiscent of a dream. What inspired those words? Feistj1I’m sorry for your loss. I had my amazing Maine Coon [cat] for 18 years before he passed away a couple of years ago. They became part of your life so it’s like letting go of a whole chapter. It’s interesting that you’ve mentioned dreams. I’m a very vivid dreamer and I have recurring places that only exist in my dreams. Sometimes music comes at me in dreams and it feels as if I’m tuned into some other channel. Once in a while I wake and think, “I’ve got to write this down”, or record it on my phone. Secret Door was one of those. I had a recurring dream where I’d go through a secret door in the woods and experience a feeling of beautiful love. The vibe came from the dream, the 3/4 time was in my head, and the bridge section came out as soon as I woke up and ran straight upstairs to work on it. A lot happens in those last moments of sleep when your mind is functional but you’re not yet in reality. It feels like a gift when that happens.

I’ve been listening to you since the beginning of your career. I wanted to be a rock singer, too, but I’ve always been told I am ugly. Show business’s obsession with beauty and sexualization to boost sales horrifies me. You make amazing music and don’t try to sell it using sexual gimmicks. Is there even the slightest chance for an unattractive woman to be a rock singer? SerbianPersonThat question makes me so sad. First of all, I would hope that whoever told you that you are ugly is not anyone you would call a friend. Don’t think of yourself that way and don’t listen to those people. They’re probably just jealous. Beauty is the deep stuff: being an artist, making music. That’s where the gold is, and beauty comes out through the inside, so focus on the inside and making something great for people to experience. Selling your product and being an Instagram star is not the important part. Anybody can make great music if it’s in your soul: that’s the most beautiful thing about you.

What is the coolest or most thoughtful gift that you have received from a fan? EvCollector87There’s been so many, but one is really special. In 2005 or so I saw this beautiful art that someone had done on the internet, a picture based on our song Imaginary. It took the lyric “in my field of paper flowers” and created a visual depiction of the song, with me laying in a field. It was just so beautiful. I managed to get in touch with them and asked if I could buy it. They told me it was a digital rendering, not a painting, but I commissioned them to paint it for me – a big version, 5ft tall or something – and it’s gorgeous. It still hangs in my space.

With the likes of Elton John, Stevie Nicks and Bruce Springsteen in mind, do you think you’ll still be recording and performing live in your 60s and 70s? ChrisDLordIf you had asked me that when we were starting out and I was in my early 20s, I would have said, hell, no. I wouldn’t have predicted we’d be here this long, but now I turn 45 in December, and 44 definitely doesn’t feel like I’d imagined – it’s better. Turning 60 is only 15 years away, which doesn’t feel that long. I don’t know if we’ll be touring hard then, but they say use it or lose it, so I’m not ruling it out. It gives you so much life to be able to bring people together and share music, so it breaks my heart to imagine that we can’t do that any more for whatever reason. I’d have to be still making music or creating in some way. It doesn’t make sense to stop.

‘Why would you want to retire me?’: Novak Djokovic is still driven by doubt

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 13:00:52 GMT

A revealing Prime Video documentary out Thursday explores the stubbornness, childhood scars and siege mentality still driving Novak Djokovic at 39

The moment comes roughly 20 minutes into the thoughtfully done Prime Video documentary, Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter, where Djokovic, winner of 24 grand slam titles and owner of the most-ever total weeks atop the ATP rankings (428), gets to the core of what has driven him to tennis royalty.

Djokovic can rightfully claim the title of the greatest male tennis player who has ever lived (“It is as clear as it gets – he is the best of all time,” Andre Agassi says in the doc) but how tennis fans feel about him has always been more complex than the universal love adorned on contemporaries Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal.

“There is a word in Serbian called inat,” Djokovic explains to the audience. “When people doubt you, when everyone is basically against you, that’s when you use that inat, that force of stubbornness to prove everybody wrong. That inat is actually quite widespread in the mentality of Serbian people.”

Inat would have been a worthy name for this 92-minute revealing exploration of Djokovic from director Jason Hehir, who has chronicled athletic giants including Michael Jordan in the Netflix/ESPN hit The Last Dance and a literal giant (HBO’s André The Giant). Hehir said that a Djokovic documentary project had been in the works since 2017, though it was first brought to him in 2023 when Sadoux Kim, one of the executive producers, took him out to lunch and explained that a film exploration of Djokovic had endured stops and starts for years. Hehir officially took on the project the following year. It debuted Thursday.

“I didn’t have specific interest in Novak as a tennis player but I knew that he had a reputation as an outspoken, often polarizing figure, and the more research I did the it felt like a great opportunity to profile a complex and compelling character,” Hehir said. “What put it over the top was the opportunity to follow a GOAT in real time.”

Hehir said he was interested in telling a story that examined Djokovic at this specific point of his career and the challenges he faced navigating a young family with the selfishness it takes to remain a champion tennis player. (Much of this story will be familiar to hardcore tennis fans; Hehir said the film was made with a global audience in mind and what is revealing is the exploration into Djokovic’s mindset rather than his biography.)

Djokovic’s wife, Jelena, offers the best psychological assessment of what drives her husband, a melange of genius, anger, playfulness and unexpressed emotions that date to his childhood in wartorn Serbia. At one point in the doc, Djokovic recalled tripping on the street in the dead of night as a young boy, unable to get the attention of his family who were running to safety, during the 1999 Nato bombings of Belgrade. Jelena describes tennis as a safe nest for her husband. “That’s the place where he finds love,” she says.

The documentary does not shy away from Djokovic’s deportation from Australia in 2022 prior to the Australian Open when the Australian government revoked his visa on the grounds that a recent Covid diagnosis did not justify an exemption to Australia’s requirement for visitors to be vaccinated.

“I never said I’m against vaccine or pro-vaccine,” Djovikic says in the doc. “The anti-vax movement claimed that I’m their hero. I’ve never associated myself with any anti-vax, pro-vax or anything. I’m pro freedom to choose what you are going to do with the integrity of your body. I missed slams and tournaments. I didn’t play in America for a couple of years because I was not vaccinated. That’s fine. But in Australia, I was allowed. I’m not the scientist, I’m not the one who is setting the rules. I’m not the one that should debate that. I stood up for what I believe in. I stand for protection of my integrity and what I think is best for my body, and that’s it.”

Djovovic is the greatest mover in the history of tennis but he cannot outrun the greatest impediment ahead of him – his age. He competed last week at the Cincinnati Open, his first tournament since Wimbledon, and was bounced in his opening match by Thiago Agustín Tirante of Argentina, the world No 50. Still, Djokovic has reached the semi-finals or better in six of his last seven grand slam tournaments and is ranked world No 5. Last month at Wimbledon he outlasted Felix Auger-Aliassime in a five-set, five-hour quarter-final epic before he was beaten by the eventual winner, Jannik Sinner. It is clear he can gear up for the big tournaments; the week-to-week stuff is much more difficult.

“I know a lot of people are retiring me already, for many years,” Djokovic says in the film. “Why would you want to retire me when I am still playing and competing at the highest level? I’m still top 5, top 10 in the world. Why would I talk about retirement when I am proving to myself that I can still win?”

Hehir said Djokovic initially did not want any mention of retirement in the documentary because he was understandably sick of addressing the subject. But the film-maker pushed Djokovic to see such questions as a compliment.

“I told Novak, “We have to address this but it’s a compliment because people are fascinated by how long you can continue to do this,’” Hehir said. “The irony here is that I think that his career is going to be elongated because of the skepticism surrounding his retirement. That’s one of the things that drives him now. I’m sure with the result in Cincinnati there will be people asking, ‘Is this the beginning of the end?’ Well, they’ve been asking this about Novak for five years. I wouldn’t be surprised at all if he made a deep run at the US Open in a few weeks.”
