Abigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a Cinzano

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 13:00:32 GMT

Harold Pinter theatre, LondonOuthwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban drama

Alison Steadman has cast a long shadow over the suburban gargoyle-cum-bored-housewife in Mike Leigh’s social satire about 1970s social mobility. So much so that her name is almost always invoked in relation to Beverly. Tamzin Outhwaite’s incredible achievement is that she banishes Steadman’s original portrayal of Bev as the definitive one.

Having first assumed the role in Nadia Fall’s 2024 production, that history shows in her polish and command of the character. The setting is a cocktail party in Essex and Outhwaite’s Bev (glittering dress, Farrah Fawcett flicks) is full of lady-of-the-manor pretensions as she serves up her officious rounds of drink. But there is a hard, calculating edge to her marital digs at estate agent husband, Laurence (Kevin Bishop) and her crude flirtation with guest Tony (Omar Malik, fantastically laconic), which she conducts with flamboyant disregard for his wife, Angela (Lauren Patel).

This seeps out early on, even before she has started to knock back the gin. She is simultaneously funny in her physical comedy and deadly serious in her put-downs of the workaholic husband who is not giving her the attention she craves, as well as her manipulations of others. Beneath her patter as party hostess is rage, hurt and an almost Madame Bovary boredom.

Her performance, and Fall’s production as a whole, proves that this period comedy of manners is eternally resonant. That is partly down to the genius of the play but Fall adds an ingenious tweak in the suggestion that Tony and Ange are of “Pakistani” origin. This transforms its meanings in a subtle but deft way: the area, we hear, is being taken over by different kinds of people and you imagine this not only being a comment on working-class mobility but racial diversity here in the “white flight” heartland of Essex. Outside Bev’s doorstep, it could be Reform Britain.

What does not work as well is the chemistry between Bev and Laurence, which lacks bite in the first act. Laurence is rather passive, and expressionless, the tension between them uncharged. The marital conflict does not seem ferocious enough for too long so you do not feel the truth of the friction between them when it bursts to the surface. They could just be George and Mildred on a bad night. In contrast, the fault-lines in Ange and Tony’s marriage are savagely revealed in his disdain of her, as much as she tries to cover it up with fake cheeriness.

It is still hugely enjoyable to see Bev flirt with the monosyllabic Tony, and to hear Ange’s inappropriate reflections on divorce in front of recently divorced neighbour, Sue (Pandora Colin).

She is the other guest at this cocktail party and the mother of eponymous punk-teen, Abigail, whose off-stage party can be heard in the background. For those who charge Leigh with othering the aspirational working-classes, not only through Bev but Laurence’s cultural snobberies, acquired in his ascension up the ladder (the framed Vincent van Gogh poster on Peter McKintosh’s orange-and-brown period set says it all), the middle-class Sue is key to Leigh’s satire. She is brilliantly portrayed as the socially-awkward, plummy ex-wife of an architect who tries to evade Laurence’s questions on the area and the class antagonisms underlying them.

He insists they listen to Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony amid the rising hysteria and the record-player is truly weaponised, Demis Roussos used to needle Laurence to the point of near-violence. Bev is a such a glorious creation that you feel her disappointments in marriage even as you gasp at her comic monstrousness. But the darkness of the ending does not land. It is partly because there are unanswered questions around their marriage but also because it has all been so enjoyably comical that this switch to tragedy leaves Bev speechless and at sea, for once.

At Harold Pinter theatre, London, until 19 September

Israel’s Ben-Gvir posts video of gallows site for hanging Palestinians

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 12:34:11 GMT

Far-right minister says those convicted in military courts of terror offences will be executed after passing of death penalty law that does not apply to Jewish extremists

Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has posted a gloating video of the construction of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – will be hanged.

Ben-Givr, who has previously attracted international sanctions and condemnation for his activities, said the new execution site would be equipped with viewing booths for families of victims to watch the hangings.

He posted the video on social media of a visit he had made to the unidentified location, where he can be seen pointing at foundations being laid and boasting it was where “terrorists will be executed”.

Photographs in the Israeli media showed a bulldozer and heavy construction work in a cordoned-off area, reportedly close to a prison.

“I promised to worsen the conditions of terrorists in prisons – we kept it,” said Ben-Gvir in the video. “I promised to pass the Death Penalty for Terrorists law – we did. And now the death row and hanging facility are also starting to take shape.”

Reports of the construction of the gallows, which will execute only Palestinians convicted of terror offences in the military courts system, and not Jewish extremists, follows the passage of a new law earlier this year. The law requires military courts to apply the death penalty as the only available sentence, unless the court finds special circumstances allowing for life imprisonment.

Jewish Israelis are in effect protected from the death penalty by a provision that applies the law only to murder committed with the “intent to deny the existence of the state of Israel”.

Ben-Gvir, who himself has convictions for incitement to racism, interfering with a police officer performing his duty, and support for a terrorist organisation (Meir Kahane’s banned Kach movement), has served as Israel’s national security minister since 2022 except for a two-month gap last year.

One of the main drivers of Israel’s new death penalty law, Ben-Gvir has a long history of extremist statements and provocations. He celebrated his 50th birthday in May with the gift of a birthday cake decorated with the iced image of a noose.

The death penalty law, one of two passed by Israeli MPs this year, has drawn widespread international condemnation since it passed the Knesset by 62 votes to 48 over allegations that it is fundamentally discriminatory.

“It also dismantles fundamental safeguards to prevent the arbitrary deprivation of life and protect the right to a fair trial, and further empowers Israel’s system of apartheid, which is maintained by scores of discriminatory laws against Palestinians,” said Erika Guevara-Rosas, a senior director at Amnesty International, when the law was passed.

Ben-Gvir in recent months became the subject of sanctions by France and Ireland in addition to UK sanctions imposed on him last year, attracted widespread criticism only days ago for advocating a policy of punitive killings in Gaza of 30-40 people a night.

“I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night,” Ben-Gvir said. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live … They are not even people.”

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, on Wednesday called Ben-Gvir’s comments “unacceptable and inhuman”, while the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said he strongly condemned “the inhumane appeals made by minister Ben-Gvir, which violate international law”.

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, ecalled Ben-Gvir’s comments “appalling”, “outrageous”, “dehumanising” and “dangerous”.

The video emerged amid growing wider international condemnation of Israel’s behaviour, including the issuing of new tenders for the massive E1 settlement block outside Jerusalem, which was denounced by the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, as an “unacceptable and destructive act” that risked separating the West Bank from East Jerusalem. He summoned Israel’s charge d’affaires in protest.

“The UK has been clear privately and publicly in our opposition to E1 and our support for a two-state solution as the only way to ensure long-term security and peace for both Palestinians and Israelis,” Miliband said. “All settlements damage that prospect and are a flagrant breach of international law.”

‘All the watering places are crammed with hot people’: on holiday with Dickens

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 12:20:19 GMT

Exhibition at Charles Dickens Museum in London looks at writer’s holiday pursuits, from Kent to the Isle of Wight

It’s summer in the city, the pubs are crowded, and the coast beckons. In a year that has so far brought five significant heatwaves, it is a fair description of the current holiday season.

But the same was true, too, of the much less frequent hot, dry summers of the past, including 186 years ago when Charles Dickens put pen to paper in anticipation of escaping London for the sea breeze in Broadstairs, Kent.

“There is no news in London – everybody is hurrying out of town – the two great theatres are shut up – and all the watering places are crammed with hot people,” he writes to his brother Alfred on 12 August 1840.

His letter, which is to go on public display for the first time, is one of several items of correspondence shedding light on Dickens and his holiday pursuits, from picnics on the Thames, beach showering on the Isle of Wight, and being ravaged by mosquitoes, bugs and other insects

“While Dickens rarely slowed down, he made sure to find time for holidays and days off, packing up plenty of his belongings and heading to the Kent coast or the West Country with his family,” said Emma Harper, deputy director at London’s Charles Dickens Museum, where the letters will go on display in the study where he wrote Oliver Twist, Nicholas Nickleby and The Pickwick Papers.

“While Dickens loved London, he was very happy to escape its crowded hot pubs for the cooler climes of the coast, or if he decided to break his routine by taking a spur of the moment day off, he would consider this a holiday. He would take his work on holiday with him and sometimes even brought his favourite pieces of furniture along so he could write from the chair and desk that suited him best.”

He positively gloated about his successful mission to construct an outdoor shower cubicle near his “very pretty” holiday cottage in Bonchurch on the Isle of Wight in 1849, expressing no qualms about spoiling the view for others. He writes to the printer William Bradbury: “We have made all visitors in search of the picturesque, mad, by putting up an immense wooden caravan on the beach, to shut in a noble waterfall and convert it into a shower bath! With some five hundred feet of fall. Which we take, every morning, to the unbounded astonishment of the aboriginal inhabitants.”

Of an 1851 trip on the Thames with his son Charley “and three other young Eton Shavers”, he promises that if his friend Thomas Beard joins them, he will be “armed with a hamper from Fortnum & Mason’s”. They can dine on a bank, “and if you can come, you and I will console ourselves for our antiquity, after dinner, with a trifle of tobacco and champagne”.

Dickens “relaxed energetically”, said Harper, and he loved to travel. To his biographer John Forster he writes of a 1842 trip to Italy: “I see myself in a striped shirt, moustache, blouse, red sash, straw hat, and white trousers, sitting astride a mule, and not caring for the clock, the day of the month, or the day of the week.”

Reflecting on one long excursion, he tells Beard in 1845 of “the gentlemanly vagabond I have been, for the last six or eight months – the extraordinary beds I have slept in – and the bewildering amount of fleas, mosquitoes, bugs, and other insects I have unwillingly bepastured – these things have hardly left me any leisure in my holiday, until within the last four or five weeks. During the whole of which time I have been employed, chiefly, in lying on my back on sofas, and leaning out of windows and over balconies, in a sort of mild intoxication.”

Summer in the City with Charles Dickens runs from 26 August to 27 September at the Charles Dickens Museum in London

There is nothing scientific about The Great ADHD Myth? ‘documentary’

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 12:18:28 GMT

Channel 4’s programme wastes a chance to ask important questions about how ADHD is diagnosed and treated, instead indulging in unscientific methods and conspiracy theories

Prof Gina Rippon is emeritus professor of cognitive neuroimaging at the Aston Brain Centre, Aston University

When Channel 4 announced that it would air a documentary titled The Great ADHD Myth?, an outpouring of fury followed. Despite this, I set out to approach it as a scientist – not just as a scientist whose own work has dealt with developmental disorders, but as someone who has enormous respect for the scientific process and for the importance of evidence-led debate.

Channel 4’s press release claimed the documentary sought to determine whether attention deficit hyperactivity disorder was a “genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or a social construct”. At one level this is a brave enterprise. ADHD is recognised worldwide as a disorder, by the World Health Organization and our own NHS among others. Estimates suggest ADHD affects roughly 8% of children and adolescents and about 3% of adults worldwide. To overturn this consensus would require robust, reproducible findings capable of explaining away decades of genetic, developmental and clinical research. The press release described the documentary as “science-led”, which hinted at just such an enterprise. Was it really science-led?

The answer is a resounding “no”. It bore little relation to a genuine scientific debate; in fact, there was no evidence of a debate at all.

One thing science tries to do is eliminate bias – not always successfully, but the intention should be there. The documentary does not start out well on this front. Max Pemberton, the presenter, has published widely about his ADHD scepticism: an article he wrote for the Daily Mail last year was headlined: “This is the REAL reason why there’s been an explosion in cases of ADHD – and why we should all be scared of the consequences.”

The very title of this programme does not promise a balanced discussion (ADHD UK has said its question mark does not serve as a “get-out-of-harm-free card”). Asking whether this is a “genuine” disorder or a “social construct” can all too easily be read as: “or made-up”.

As the late physicist Richard Feynman pointed out, good science should be as ruthless with the evidence that supports your thesis as it is with the evidence that contradicts it. This “documentary” (having seen it, I am deliberately putting this term in scare quotes) doesn’t report any evidence that might contradict the conclusion it has clearly reached at the outset. Not only that, the “evidence” (ditto) it does present mostly comprises a series of trenchant opinions from carefully selected talking heads, and focuses on a couple of so-called experiments that break just about every rule of genuine scientific inquiry.

Is ADHD a “genuine developmental disorder”? Setting aside the support from the likes of the WHO and Nice, as well as powerful genetic evidence unmentioned in the documentary, the presenter decided that if we could “see” ADHD in the brain, this might prove it to be genuine. He interrogated Prof Katya Rubia, a cognitive neuroscientist who does have a genuine track record in ADHD research. She reported that key differences had been spotted at the group level and added that they were small. A landmark study in 2017, combining MRI data from more than 3,000 people, reports just such findings. Pemberton missed the point she was making, and asked that perennially naive question that plagues brain imagers: can you “spot” ADHD in a single scan, or use it for a diagnosis? In response to her honest answer, no (which is exactly what you might expect, confronted with a single example from an enormously heterogeneous population), he appeared to conclude that if there was no brain-based marker that distinguished a brain with ADHD from one without, ADHD could not be a brain-based disorder. And, therefore it was not a genuine developmental disorder.

Apparently, this means ADHD is a social construct – even if the evidence in favour of that conclusion is deeply flawed. Opinions about screen time and ultra-processed food and big pharma conspiracy theories were wheeled out in support of this claim, as well as scornful references to diagnostic manuals, this time without any attempt to offer supporting evidence. The presentation of “genuine” condition or “social construct” as a simple binary choice harked back to the old “nature or nurture” debates, with no acknowledgment of contemporary findings about the entanglement between the brain and its world. Just because you believe that something “out there” is responsible for certain kinds of behaviour, it doesn’t mean that the brain is not involved.

At the heart of the programme were two so-called “carefully monitored experiments”. One involved a 10-year-old boy, Mason, being taken off his medication for six weeks. He was not randomly selected but “volunteered” by his mother, who felt that the medication was masking the real Mason. In addition to stopping the medication, a holistic practitioner removed items such as screens and mobile phones, ultra-processed food and chocolate, and suggested walks in nature, exercise and yoga. The consequences of this were reported throughout the programme.

This was not a scientific experiment in any sense. Setting aside the fact that a case study such as this would not produce any kind of reliable evidence, you could point out that there were no “control” conditions. Was there a child taken off their meds but not offered holistic alternatives? Was there a child who stayed on their meds, but was also offered alternatives? One could go on. Mason’s story is powerful television because it is complicated, human and emotionally engaging. Those are not, unfortunately, the usual ingredients of a controlled experiment.

Pemberton’s own contribution comprised a demonstration of the diagnostic process. After handing over £1,200 for a private online assessment, he triumphantly reported that he had (almost instantaneously) been diagnosed with ADHD. He seemed to conclude that ADHD therefore could not be a valid clinical construct. Setting aside, again, the non-contribution of an anecdote such as this to a genuinely science-led inquiry, his conclusion seems to be that if you can wrongly get an ADHD diagnosis, then ADHD can’t be real. It is worth noting that his foray into costly online clinics bears no resemblance to the immensely painstaking procedures behind an ADHD diagnostic procedure as laid out by Nice guidelines. Yet again, Pemberton displayed a warped non-scientific logic. A diagnostic process being flawed does not mean the construct it is trying to measure does not exist.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The frustrating thing about The Great ADHD Myth? is that buried inside it are several questions that science really does need to ask. Are diagnostic thresholds becoming too broad? Are all private assessments rigorous enough? Are drugs sometimes used where environmental changes would be better? Do schools demand an unnecessarily narrow range of behaviour from children? And do we know enough about the long-term effects of stimulant medication? These are important questions. But none require us to pretend that decades of genetic, developmental, clinical and neuroscientific evidence simply disappear.

There is nothing unscientific about questioning ADHD. Science progresses by questioning accepted wisdom. But genuine scientific scepticism means subjecting your preferred explanation to the strongest evidence against it. It does not mean assembling a procession of experts and anecdotes that point in the same direction and calling the result “science-led”.

Prof Gina Rippon is emeritus professor of cognitive neuroimaging at the Aston Brain Centre, Aston University, and the author of The Gendered Brain

Hazy sunshine, factor-50 smiles and Cliff Richard at the wheel: the 20 best summer holiday movies – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 12:05:39 GMT

From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal moment

Let’s begin at the end. 2 September 1962: the final night of the summer vacation; one last big blowout before adult life intervenes. George Lucas’s rambunctious salute to footloose youth paints vivid vignettes of Modesto, California, rocking around the clock with its loose-knit gaggle of characters. But this has one eye on the meter and knows that time is running short.

“It’s a working holiday,” insists Olivia Colman’s brittle academic, blasting her factor-50 smile at the bemused guests and staff of a Greek island resort. She’s in flight from her past and liable to combust any second. Paradise here offers little rest or respite. The professor has made a clean getaway, but she’s brought along all her baggage.

In which Natalie Press’s working-class Yorkshire lass finds an exotic foreign land just a hop and a skip across the moor in the form of the ivy-clad house of Emily Blunt’s boarding-school princess. Director Paweł Pawlikowski slowly turns up the temperature as the girls lean into the season, lounging in the dry grass and listening to Edith Piaf. They’re at once stickily close and a thousand miles apart.

David Lean’s tender Technicolor romance was one of the first British films to be shot entirely on location, strolling around beautiful, dirty Venice in the company of Katharine Hepburn’s middle-aged Miss Lonelyheart. Lean called for her to step backwards into the green canal at Campo San Barnaba. Hepburn gamely obliged and clambered out with conjunctivitis.

Sex and death ride shotgun in Alfonso Cuarón’s lustful field trip through turn-of-the-century Mexico. Gael García Bernal and Diego Luna are teenage buddies who light out for the beach with their engines overheating; Maribel Verdú co-stars as the exacting older woman who, if not quite steering them straight, at least helps point them in interesting new directions.

A summer holiday list without Summer Holiday? It would be like the Tower without the ravens or mistletoe without the wine. Directed with an easy swing by Peter Yates (his debut, and he would go on to make Bullitt and Breaking Away), this now stands as a colourful blast from the past, an innocent postcard from postwar, pre-Brexit Europe. A blue-collar bus mechanic – embodied by Cliff Richard – magics up a new route from Hertfordshire down to Athens, complete with entertainment and a flurry of comic misadventures. Only a churl wouldn’t get on board.

Céline Sciamma makes small rousing films about secret lives, sanctuaries and precious stolen moments. Tomboy is one of her best: a gorgeous coming-of-age tale about 10-year-old Laure (Zoé Héran), who – bouncing between schools, the new kid on the block – introduces herself as Mickaël and effectively becomes another person. Sciamma’s implied message? That the humble summer break can be a transformational timeout, with September’s child only distantly related to July’s.

The pool is a mirror in Jacques Deray’s dazzling, depthless thriller pungently set on the French Riviera and tapping the off-screen tensions of co-stars Romy Schneider and Alain Delon. If La Piscine’s air of modish ennui now feels overused, that’s because it’s a design classic, most notably lifted and adapted by both François Ozon’s Swimming Pool and Luca Guadagnino’s A Bigger Splash.

“Rome. By all means, Rome,” declares Audrey Hepburn’s runaway princess after spending a liberative, life-changing few days in the eternal city with Gregory Peck’s US newsman. As for the movie, this might be the ultimate European and American meet-cute. Shot on location, skipping between the tourist sights, Roman Holiday wedded old-school Hollywood romance with the looser rhythm of Italian neorealism.

Eric Rohmer was the poet laureate of French dreamers, the creator of films that feel flyweight and then linger for a lifetime. A Summer’s Tale is his semi-autobiographical account of a lost summer spent on the coast of Brittany pursuing sea shanties and women with the same awkward stumble. It’s a hazy, lazy joy of a film, brimming with sunlight and rocked by the backwash of chatter and song.

Everything’s big in this Borscht Belt summer classic. Big gestures, big emotions, big drums on the soundtrack, big hair. It’s 1963 and Baby (Jennifer Grey) is getting whisked off her feet by Patrick Swayze’s bad-boy dance instructor. The Catskills are a cauldron of class and ethnic tensions; first love is an intoxicating, disorientating hot mess. Resistance is futile: the film lifts and spins us. Grand finale, big reward.

The best holidays are the ones that you never, ever want to end. Michel Franco’s Sundown casts Tim Roth as mild-mannered Neil, whose Mexican vacation is interrupted by the news of his mother’s sudden death. The trouble is that Neil would really prefer not to leave. So he pretends he’s lost his passport, shoves his tear-stained family through the departure gate and then circles back to the beach with the satisfied air of a man who’s just put out all the bins. Who is this Neil? What the hell is he thinking? He’s the shadow beneath the parasol, the chip of ice in the cocktail glass and the finest existential antihero this side of L’Étranger.

LP Hartley’s source novel was elegant and reflective, weighed down by the heat as it traces the illicit exchange of letters via a lovestruck schoolboy. Joseph Losey and Harold Pinter make the mood more jangly and atonal, perpetually on the verge of panic. What a wonderfully treacherous period drama this is, the filmic equivalent of a strip of flypaper. All the characters are stuck and squirming. None of them are getting away unscathed.

This was initially lower on the list, as befits its musty antique status, but then I watched it again and it’s flawless – there’s nothing else quite like it. Jacques Tati is the hapless holidaymaker who haunts the wings of a seaside town sometimes as a mute witness, sometimes as an agent of gentle chaos. If anything, Tati’s comedy grows more cherishable with each passing decade. Watching it is like peering into a forgotten tide-pool ecosystem: the rumble-tumble lost world of the postwar French resort.

Where its spiritual ancestor, American Graffiti, began at the end, the uproarious Dazed and Confused wraps up at the start. It’s the first full day of the 1976 summer break. The high-school kids are wafting groggily back to earth, buffeted and elated after a wild night around town. They’ve drunk beer and shot pool, run amok and made out, and now there’s nothing on the horizon except an Aerosmith concert and the month of June. Sunrise on the football field; the golden morning of their lives.

Flee your family, feel the city; steer a boat around the archipelago. Ingmar Bergman’s jolting kitchen-sink romance casts Harriet Andersson and Lars Ekborg as working-class Stockholm kids who make a bold bid for freedom and yet are bound for the rocks. Bergman was always drawn to life’s extremes – its sunlight and shadow, its ecstasies and agonies – but rarely made them feel as purely relatable as here.

Forget the beach and the island retreat – it is the forest where summer breaks tend to deepen and darken. Four Kolkata bachelors drive into the backwoods of Bihar only to realise that there is more than one way to get lost. What follows is an antic meditation on all the big stuff: friendship, responsibility, class and cultural divisions. Writer-director Satyajit Ray takes a humdrum off-the-peg concept – the buddy hangout comedy – and makes it mythic, mysterious and borderline elemental.

The second Rohmer film on the list is a small miracle about a small miracle. Specifically it’s about thirtysomething Delphine (Marie Rivière), who is newly single and drifting in a kind of semi-ostracised state across France. But it is also about the green ray, which can reputedly be glimpsed for a split second at sunset and might quietly, magically make everything right. Rohmer employed a skeleton crew and encouraged his cast to improvise, ensuring that his film remained unencumbered and almost weightless, open to the world’s possibilities and the happy accidents it might send our way.

Charlotte Wells’s rapturous family album is still relatively recent and may yet fade out as the years go by. Then again maybe not, because if Aftersun tells us anything it’s that memory only intensifies an experience and that lost summers burn brighter the older we get. On screen it’s for ever 1999 and Paul Mescal’s young father is in Turkey with his daughter (Frankie Corio), browsing for rugs and lounging by the pool, searching for sunshine and averting their gaze from the shadows. Wells’s astonishing debut feature doesn’t feel directed so much as recovered and resurrected. It’s an impressionistic, deeply felt and finally devastating tour de force.

The summer holiday can be a time of freedom and escape, romance and self-discovery. It is all of these things in Richard Linklater’s mid-90s masterpiece about a pair of garrulous Interrailers (Julie Delpy and Ethan Hawke) who steal a few precious hours and wander around Vienna for the night. But the best summer holiday movies are also about time itself. They’re about how we choose to use it and what comes out of those choices.

Before Sunrise, a joyous film about footloose youth, tellingly went on to spark a pair of excellent sequels that caught up with its lovers many years down the line. But that awareness of time was baked into the tale from the start. I agonised at some length over what should be number one on this list – and what probably swung it was the bittersweet flourish of Before Sunrise’s last moments, when Linklater’s camera beats back like a ghost to show us the places where Céline and Jesse were idling just a few hours before. The fountain and the ferris wheel. The forlorn little alley with the stacked wooden pallets. The Interrailers have already left them behind and moved on – except that they haven’t, not really. They’ll be haunting them happily for the rest of their lives.

Humans have learned to fear ‘bugs’, but we shouldn’t – life as we know it hinges on invertebrates

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 11:00:50 GMT

At this point of the crisis in our relations with the natural world, we’ve got to protect these creatures – and we are running out of time

Read more from the Guardian’s invertebrate of the year 2026

Too many animals are regarded as “bugs”. And, if anything is a bug, it is a short step to it becoming a “pest”. Too many of us have a learned fear – it’s not innate – of anything with six legs or antennae.

I’m a big fan of the invertebrates and I love the Guardian’s invertebrate of the year competition because it focuses people’s attention on the little things rather than the typical animal superstars – the pandas, tigers and orangutans. In their diversity and varied ecology, the million-plus invertebrates on our planet often lead far more intricate and interesting lives than large animals with spines, like us. We urgently need to generate a much broader awareness of their beauty and importance. All these small creatures are as integral a part of our ecosystems as the fluffy things that we may want to put on our calendars.

I’ve always tried to champion invertebrates on Springwatch. One of my greatest joys filming the series over the years was meeting a naturalist who knew about tree slugs. I’d spent my life looking at trees with slime trails going up their trunks but I’d never bothered to get a ladder and investigate. So the discovery that every night these slugs venture out and climb to the tops of oak trees and then slither back down again before dawn breaks is amazing. And it’s all happening just over the fence.

I’m 65 and the other day I caught an insect in my kitchen that I’d never before thought to identify. It turned out to be a parasitic wasp, one of more than 330 species of netelia, a genus of ichneumonid wasps. It was a cinnamon colour, with huge eyes because it is nocturnal and parasitises large moth caterpillars. It actually packs a powerful sting for humans, which I had no idea about. We are constantly learning about the miraculous alternative worlds unfolding all around us. In this invertebrate universe, there is an enormous repository of fascination just waiting to be discovered.

I have previously encountered the third-placed invertebrate in this year’s competition. I once visited a beach in Florida where horseshoe crabs had spawned and died. There were so many that you couldn’t walk on the beach. It was like some sort of Jurassic apocalypse. Absolutely extraordinary.

I didn’t know much about this year’s winner, the leaf sheep, until it appeared on the Guardian shortlist. Then I read up on it a bit more. Physically, they are one of these animals that might as well come from another planet; they have an amazing structure and life cycle. Taking in algae and using it to power yourself – only four and a half billion years of evolution could come up with something that wacko. It’s absolutely brilliant.

Learning about these animals and celebrating them is important, but we want to know what we can do to help them too. The tempting thing to say is plant nectar sources and allow your garden to go a bit wild, if you’re lucky enough to have a garden. We take joy in making spaces for these creatures in our local neighbourhoods and that’s a battle, but it’s not going to win the war.

We are running out of time – and here in the UK, we’ve got to lobby for better pesticide regulations. They’ve done it in France and reduced pesticide use on farmland. We banned insect-killing neonicotinoids in 2018 and yet this year, they have again been approved for “emergency” use on sugar beet crops. This should be causing an outcry. We need the public to pressurise the government into reforming and reducing pesticide usage.

We need a wider public awareness of them and their importance if we want invertebrate life and therefore the bats and birds and everything else – including us – to prosper. Winner of Invertebrate of the Year 2026 crowned – and it is the size of a grain of rice

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 11:00:50 GMT

The leaf sheep, a neon green solar-powered slug, has inspired at least one Pokémon character and triumphs in global ballot

See the top 10 shortlist here

Chris Packham: ‘Life as we know it hinges on invertebrates’

A neon green solar-powered slug that lives underwater is the winner of the increasingly popular Invertebrate of the Year competition run by the Guardian.

The leaf sheep, Costasiella kuroshimae, triumphed in the global ballot after hundreds of thousands of readers around the world read about and shared their appreciation for the spineless creatures who make up the majority of animal life on Earth.

Announcing the winner, the broadcaster and environmental campaigner Chris Packham said: “It’s very, very beautiful but also very smart too. It harvests photosynthetic material from the algae it feeds upon and builds its own solar panels.”

In a much closer contest than previous years – when the tardigrade and the common earthworm won with popular landslides – the beady-eyed, charming leaf sheep fought off strong competition from the world’s largest bumblebee, the moscardón, Bombus dahlbomii, which finished second. This giant ginger bumblebee is increasingly threatened in its native Patagonia because of invasive bumblebee species introduced by humans in recent decades.

In third place was the horseshoe crab, a remarkable arthropod that pre-dates the dinosaurs and contains blue blood, closely followed by the common woodlouse.

Although worms have historically polled very strongly in the competition, bringing up the rear in 10th place on this year’s shortlist was the astonishing bootlace worm, one of the longest animals in the world.

The competition was launched three years ago to celebrate overlooked and often derided invertebrates, who number at least 1.7m species – about 97% of all animals – with probably millions more still to be discovered and described by science. Without the unpaid labour of wild invertebrates who pollinate crucial crops, filter water, recycle waste, clean up pollution and add fertility to soils, human life on Earth would quickly perish.

This year, several thousand spineless candidates nominated by Guardian readers, including everyone from scientists to children, were whittled down to a shortlist of 10.

As each candidate was announced during a two-week fiesta of invertebrate appreciation, experts offered their perspectives with Erica McAlister extolling the importance – and beauty – of flies, the wildlife photographer Dara Ojo revealing the joys of macro photography, and Connor Butler pointing out how there is no “other” in the natural world: we are all part of the same living systems.

The leaf sheep, which lives in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines, was only first described by science in 1993. Since then, it has become increasingly celebrated in human culture thanks to advances in underwater macro photography that have revealed its remarkably cute appearance, which has inspired at least one Pokémon character.

‘It was a damn unicorn’: the pioneering, divisive power of Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 09:00:48 GMT

On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classic

It was the summer of 1984 and things weren’t going well for Paul Simon. The year prior, a blockbuster Simon and Garfunkel tour ended in bickering. Meanwhile, even though the 1980 single Late in the Evening reached the US Top 10, Simon’s last two albums had not sold very well, and his marriage to Carrie Fisher was starting to unravel. In the midst of all that the 43-year-old folk icon was steadily working on building a beach home out on the far end of Long Island.

Many of Simon’s pilgrimages from Manhattan out to Montauk were soundtracked by a bootleg tape of accordion-heavy mbaqanga, a South African music style with jazz rhythms and bright guitar chords, he had received from a friend. It was on those drives that the seeds of Graceland, the crown jewel of Simon’s discography, were planted. “Many of us, in that day and age, found a moment of self-reflection – of being able to go deep inside ourselves – when we were in the car on these road trips,” said Ashley Kahn, whose new book, Days of Miracle and Wonder, follows the gestation process of Graceland. “If it wasn’t the radio, it was cassettes.”

Forty years on, Graceland remains the most nimble, ecstatic album that Simon’s hands have touched. It’s constructed around contributions from South African musicians whose “township jive” reminded Simon of the early rock and doowop records he heard as a kid in Queens. There’s musical detours of all kinds – a trip to Louisiana inspired Simon to record with zydeco group Rockin’ Dopsie and the Zydeco Twisters, while the song All Around the World or the Myth of Fingerprints features Los Lobos’ fusion of norteño and rock. Simon is at his best when among resonant rhythms from Johannesburg.

Inspired by the bootleg, Simon booked jam sessions in Johannesburg with different bands – General MD Shirinda and the Gaza Sisters, Tao Ea Matsekha, the Boyoyo Boys – where he developed melodies and scribbled down lyrics as engineer Roy Halee tracked the groups’ grooves. Some of the songs that ended up on Graceland were assembled on top of these groups’ already-finished songs, such as Gumboots, a thrilling pop confection that Simon initially heard as an instrumental on that tape. For Simon, whose process often started with an acoustic guitar, it was a profound shift in how he approached his craft. “He’s finding a way of building from the rhythm up; that, for him, was profoundly new,” said Kahn, who compared Simon’s then-newfound process with hip-hop: “Start with the beat and match the words to the beat.”

In these February 1985 sessions, Simon had found a surge of inspiration, but the harsh realities of South African apartheid loomed outside the studio doors. After dark, the Black musicians weren’t allowed on the streets of Johannesburg, nor were they allowed to use public transportation. As a result, a day of recording would reach an “uncomfortable time when the players couldn’t concentrate until they knew there might be a car to take them home”, Simon told Rolling Stone in 1986. In a foreshadowing of the backlash Graceland would go on to receive, the manager of the Soul Brothers told Simon he believed recording in South Africa constituted a violation of the United Nations’ 1980 boycott, which was passed to prevent the South African government from using culture as propaganda for apartheid.

Kahn believes that Simon had the musicians’ labor rights in mind. “He wanted to have them participate, he wanted them to be credited and he wanted them to be compensated,” said Kahn, emphatically noting that Simon paid the South African musicians triple the daily rate of musicians in American unions. “Did he do it perfectly? No. But there wasn’t a set formula of how to approach this.” Simon has still faced backlash over the years about Graceland’s songwriting credits from several musicians who appeared on the album, including Los Lobos, Rockin’ Dopsie and the Zydeco Twisters, and even guitarist Ray Phiri, who helped construct the album’s title track. Against charges of cultural appropriation, Graceland advocates have suggested that Simon’s work in South Africa helped bring these bands, such as Ladysmith Black Mambazo, who round out the starry-eyed Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes, to a larger audience.

Before the first sessions at Ovation Studios in Johannesburg, Simon spoke with calypso legend Harry Belafonte, who had suggested that he reach out to the African National Congress. Believing that the power of art trumped laws, Simon resisted Belafonte’s recommendation. Months after the release of Graceland, the UN’s special committee against apartheid censured Simon and planned to add him to the list of performers who violated the boycott. “They were looking for a coordinated message, coordinated push, hence the issue with the boycott,” Kahn added. The UN’s decision was reversed months later when Simon wrote a letter to the committee noting that he had understood the ban focused on performing, not recording, and he had no intentions of performing in South Africa.

A career-long tug-of-war between Simon’s cerebral and conversational language courses through Graceland. He eschewed overt anti-apartheid protest songs, but the anxieties of his experience in South Africa seep into Homeless and The Boy in the Bubble, which opens on an image of “the soldiers by the side of the road” while the interplay between famo-style accordion and bass suggests something threatening up ahead. But Simon’s qualms – his failed marriage, his feelings about being washed up, his worries related to the information age – are what he fleshes out on Graceland, often through dizzying images (“lasers in the jungle”) or larger-then-life characters (“Fat Charlie the Archangel”).

“One of the images that always comes to me is Paul in a room with a rubber ball – bouncing it, bouncing it, bouncing it – to get into a Zen-like state where lyrics start to come,” Kahn said. “He’s already thinking about songwriting. The lyrics are there. He just needs to silence all the other shit that’s in one’s mind.”

Graceland’s steady stream of longing, sometimes offered through simple lines such as “You don’t feel you could love me but I feel you could,” contained unexpected emotional wallops. On the album’s very best songs, there’s an impressionistic flow of feeling in Simon’s lyrics. Nowhere is that clearer than in the title track, where the word Graceland had initially been written down as a placeholder. It eventually evolved into a figurative destination for Simon as he tried to mend his broken heart after his marriage to Fisher. “If I miss in the direction of head, I risk being obscure or pretentious,” Simon said in 1986. “If I miss in the direction of heart, I risk being sentimental. I dread both. I dance in the penumbra. That’s the thrill. When it’s right, I can feel it.”

Many revisions and additions happened stateside, including the guitar-synth textures from Adrian Belew and Steve Gadd’s AMS reverb-drenched drums on All Around the World. For another set of sessions, including the one in which they rerecorded You Can Call Me Al, Simon flew Phiri, Bakithi Kumalo – whose restless fretless bass is now synonymous with the Graceland album – and drummer Isaac Mtshali to New York, where Simon also shared his progress with David Byrne, Cyndi Lauper and Philip Glass. He would turn on a tape of an instrument track, get close to their ears and sing the melodies or lyrics he’d crafted. “The fact that Paul was open to sharing the process with a lot of people goes to show a certain strength, as well as an openness to saying, ‘I could be wrong,’ or, ‘I could be better,’” Kahn says.

Graceland’s influence as a genre-defying, cross-pollinated album has spread far and wide, informing brilliant artists such as Vampire Weekend and Lorde, plus with one particular viral parody of Simon’s approach. For almost as long as the album has been in stores, a healthy dose of criticism has followed: two decades before he would produce for Beyoncé and Eminem, a young Mark Batson asked Simon how he could justify “taking over this music”, before discussing how Black art has been “stolen” by white artists time and time again during a Q&A at Howard University. It’s a testament to the life-affirming melodies and jubilant grooves of Graceland that it hasn’t been consigned to the dust bin of history as an embarrassment – and that these conversations endure. “All these questions about appropriation, about systemic racist, about the entitled versus the non-entitled – that’s never going away,” Kahn says. “What Graceland did was show us a way to talk about it.”

It’s hard to imagine when Graceland arrived in stores towards the end of August 1986 that it wasn’t an overnight sensation. Support from music critics, performances on Saturday Night Live and eventually Grammy wins helped it find an audience. (It entered the Billboard 200 album chart at No 94 in September 1986, before eventually peaking at No 3 next April, just over a month after the Grammys ceremony.) The final piece of the puzzle was pop radio programmers, who didn’t understand the stylistic jumps taking place across Graceland. The spring after the album’s release, radio honchos latched onto its lead single, You Can Call Me Al, with its attempts to find salvation in the “angels in the architectures”. It was a classic case of better late than never: “It was a damn unicorn,” Kahn says. “In the zoo of music, they had no idea which cage to put it in.”

Days of Miracle and Wonder: Paul Simon and the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland by Ashley Kahn is out now

To Iran’s political prisoners, trapped ‘between two blades of a scissors’

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 09:00:48 GMT

On one side, you face the domination of the Islamic Republic; on the other, the imperialist forces that republic claims to stand against

August marks the anniversary of the 1988 mass executions in Iran, a horror that echoes in the country’s current surge in death sentences. It also marks the 19 August anniversary of the UK- and US-orchestrated coup against the prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh in 1953. Amid the current, indiscriminate waves of US-Israeli military assaults against Iran, this letter of solidarity denounces the repression of the Iranian people and their political prisoners by forces both at home and abroad.

To our fellow activists, students, thinkers, workers, artists, and other prisoners of conscience held behind the walls of all detention centers across Iran:

We write to you from a place of deep solidarity, our hearts heavy with the knowledge of the struggle you face within Iran’s prisons: the torture, the systematic neglect, the enforced silence, and the brutal reality of sham trials and executions. As former and current political prisoners, activists, and scholars committed to the global project of abolition, anti-authoritarianism and anti-imperialism, we see you across the distances of geography and the silence of censorship and internet blackouts. And we stand in solidarity with you, as you are at the intersection of two sources of oppression.

On one side, you face the Islamic Republic that, from its inception, enforced absolute social and political control based on an exclusionary ideology. It is a system that claims to counter imperial power while using its very logic of domination and systems of carcerality, torture and execution. On the other side, you face the aggression and violence of the very imperialist and Zionist forces the Islamic Republic purports to stand against. The US and Israel instigate brutal wars, destroy civilian infrastructure, kill innocent schoolgirls, and treat you as collateral damage in their pursuit of regional dominance. We remember the horror of 23 June 2025, when Israel struck the Evin prison complex, flattening its hospital ward, transgender section, and visitor center. You best exposed this dual oppression when you voiced that you “feel stuck between the two blades of a scissors, the evil regime that imprisons and tortures [you] and a foreign force dropping bombs on [your] heads in the name of freedom”.

In the past year, we witnessed both blades of the scissor sharpen. We see the arbitrary arrests and the horrific wave of state executions. We see the deepening criminalization of the working class and unemployed, the targeting of Kurds, Arabs, and Baloch, and the scapegoating of Afghan migrants: all desperate attempts to kill the spirit of people they cannot contain. This is the logic of carceral states everywhere: when they fail to address the crises people face, they simply attempt to criminalize or disappear the people themselves.

We see the same logic of domination when Israel uses “administrative detention” to hold Palestinian political prisoners for years without charge. We see it when Israeli authorities celebrate a new law that allows them to execute the Palestinian political prisoners they cannot dominate. We see it in the ICE detention centers where the US government imprisons our people in the pursuit of a political agenda of racist exclusion or detains our political activists for daring to speak against the US-backed Israeli genocide. We see it in the history of the US targeting freedom fighters, particularly Black, Indigenous, Puerto Rican and other anticolonial organizers, locking them away for decades to crush movements for national liberation and sovereignty. And we see the connections between these carceral systems sharing intelligence and governance techniques, such as when the USP Marion prison in Illinois became a blueprint for prisons built in Iran and Israel in the 1960s. Whether it is a border wall or a prison gate, the goal is the same: to silence people through fear, domination, and isolation.

Your struggle is as global as our collective dreams of freedom and dignity. We stand with you, and we reject the false binary of imperialism and hollow anti-imperialism. We invite global civil society and anti-imperialist activists and organizations to extend their unconditional support and solidarity to all incarcerated kin fighting for our collective liberation, to build relationships with Iranian political prisoners and uplift their voices, to put pressure on the Islamic Republic by challenging its narrative, and to call upon that government to immediately stop all the executions and free all political prisoners.

The Iranian authorities must stop their inhumane practice of death and incarceration now. And the US and Israel must end their barbaric wars and brutal sanctions that knowingly devastate our communities.

In solidarity and with love,

Alberto Toscano, emeritus professor of critical theory, Goldsmiths, *University of London

Angela Davis, former political prisoner, distinguished professor emerita, *University of California, Santa Cruz

Bernardine Dohrn, retired professor of law, *Northwestern University

Relax, everyone: Elon Musk has a mantra to make the climate crisis go away

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 07:00:45 GMT

It’s simple, says the SpaceX boss – according to something called the ‘Kardashev scale’, we just have to move energy production ‘off-planet’

Next time the weather gives the UK 61 days without rain and we wonder idly if this is the end, there is a term we may whistle up to soothe us. Like murmuring the rosary, or putting our fingers in our ears and humming, this phrase is to be mumbled on repeat – “the Kardashev scale, the Kardashev scale” – a buzzy concept in tech, much favoured by Elon Musk, and precisely the thing we’ve been waiting for. The Kardashev scale is the answer both to our impending doom and our anxiety around it – and if we decide to believe in it, we won’t have to give the climate crisis a single thought until the last drip falls from the tap.

This is the idea and it’s a familiar one to anyone who has watched tech billionaires take intractable, commonplace crises and decide that, among the measures and proposals in play, the vital missing ingredient so far has been them. Do you remember when Jeff Bezos, rather than doing something quotidian and loserish like funding public education by ensuring Amazon pays the same tax rate as regular Americans, decided instead to reinvent preschools?

Or Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, who also set up some schools – no expertise required, just a reach-for-the-stars attitude and a passion for change. At the risk of sounding callous, one might even put Steve Jobs’s eschewing of traditional cancer treatment in this category; after he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2003, the founder of Apple delayed surgery in favour of his own holistic and dietary remedies. None of these ventures has been successful.

We know what this is: the default belief held by tech billionaires that their particular brilliance is a kind of skeleton key for all human knowledge, past, present and future, rocket-fuelled by innovation and untethered from the limitations that come with the dull, plodding alternative: that of actually knowing stuff about a specialist subject. If they offer a magic bullet for any number of problems, the appeal to the rest of us is powerful. Who among us, when booking a flight or glancing up at another cloudless sky, hasn’t thought guiltily, oh, well, at some point someone will, like, invent a shield or something, and everything will turn out OK.

Which brings us to the Kardashev scale, named for the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev, who in 1964 invented a rubric to measure the success of any civilisation based on its ability to harness energy. Kardashev came up with a sliding scale of energy usage on which humanity had not reached even “type I” according to his measurements – because we can neither control the weather nor fully harness the energy of the sun. The highest level in this schema was a type III, which describes a civilisation that has harnessed the energy of the galaxy – and above that further theoretical levels, including a type IV (the energy of the universe) and type V (the multiverse) to hold up against our dimwit civilisation’s current reliance on fossil fuels.

You can see why this appeals in Silicon Valley: the Kardashev scale has a kind of nostalgic futurism about it familiar to any student of the space race or the works of L Ron Hubbard, and leans on fun terms such as “galactic”, “space-time” and “moon bases”. If this isn’t blue-sky thinking, I don’t know what is, and Musk has launched into it. He has suggested that a natural implementation of Kardashev’s ideas is to develop space infrastructure – in effect moving energy production “off-planet”, along with orbital datacentres – by launching millions of units into orbit to better capture the energy of the sun.

It sounds super cool. And while visionaries need vast ambition and an ability to withstand ridicule, these proposals demand a willing suspension of disbelief from us, too. If you don’t, for example, let your mind drift back to that time Musk had Tesla engineers design a tiny submarine to fetch those kids trapped in a cave, or to whatever it was he did at the US “department of government efficiency” (Doge) that everyone in the Republican party now seems keen to pretend never happened, you can persuade yourself that the creator of Starlink might be on to something. The Kardashev scale, the Kardashev scale – don’t you feel better already?

From bone-dry to soaked to the bone, welcome to the age of climate whiplash

The Guardian Thu, 20 Aug 2026 05:00:43 GMT

This punishingly hot and dry summer will probably be followed by another wet winter. But it’s nothing compared with what Britain will endure in years to come

This summer could be the hottest, driest and deadliest in English history. Successive heatwaves have so far claimed almost 3,000 lives. Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales is in drought, while key reservoirs are parched. Across this brown and stickily unpleasant land, from Grimsby down to St Ives, hosepipe bans are in force, while music festivals are staged not on green fields but in giant dust bowls.

Just how bad is it? I asked a leading climate scientist.

“This is as good as it’s going to get,” said Hayley Fowler, a professor at Newcastle University. “It will only get hotter.”

A little while back, the Met Office filmed a mock weather forecast for 2050, with an authoritative yet smiley man wielding a clicker in front of a map. So far, so soothingly familiar – only the UK had gone from its usual green and jaunty yellow to a deep, bloody red. Cambridge was stamped with 40C, while Somerset and Dorset were up at 45C. This is the near-future that awaits you and me, our children and grandchildren. Just two decades away, the weather forecaster urged us to block out the sun and stay indoors. “Drink plenty of fluids,” he added.

Except there will not be as much fluid to drink. Britain is world-renowned for its soft steady drizzle, but over the next couple of decades, our summers will turn arid while winters are more likely to bring a regular deluge of rain, breaking our riverbanks and flooding our homes. Indeed, El Niño means this winter is likely to be especially bad – up there with Storm Desmond, believed Prof Fowler, the cyclone that in December 2015 shut down railway lines and plunged more than 60,000 homes in the north of England into darkness with no power.

“Climate whiplash”, scientists call this: lurching from bone-dry to soaked to the bone. Pleading for water half the year, then terrified of its power the other half. This is not “climate change” as it used to be shown on official graphs, running on smooth lines pointing upwards; this is breakdown.

Not that you’d know it from our politicians. This week, Nigel Farage’s useful idiot, Richard Tice, urged us to stop moaning and down some English sparkling. Our new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is strikingly eloquent on many subjects, but keeps stumm on the climate crisis, apart from his promises to be “pragmatic” on fossil fuels. Elsewhere, the columnists dust off their standby paragraphs fulminating about the Englishman’s right to wash his own SUV, and the public information ads chide us to turn off taps, as if more mindful toothbrushing is a climate-adaptation strategy. All is business as usual – even while the business model is broken.

“We are used to taking water for granted, thinking of it as infinitely available,” Dr Jonathan Paul, an earth scientist at Royal Holloway University of London, told me. “Very soon, we will be treating it as a precious resource.” He can foresee battles for who gets water between farmers and datacentres.

At the start of this year, I wrote about the temporary drought faced by households in Kent and Sussex, thousands of whom faced no running water for days on end. In Tunbridge Wells, people told me how quickly social norms broke down. Washing from buckets, they spent their days feeling grubby and smelly. Supermarkets were stripped bare of water.

Readers wrote to me about how those everyday scenes struck them as frightening, but they are what lies ahead for many more of us, if we leave a looming water crisis to be solved by our busted water system. Britain’s water supply is entrusted to a string of local private monopolies, overseen by underfunded, demoralised and largely toothless watchdogs. Since Margaret Thatcher sold off our water, this essential infrastructure has fallen into the hands of a transnational network of spivs and cowboys who have stripped it of almost every penny. For the sake of elite enrichment and lower household bills, the water system has relied on the public investment made by postwar social-democratic governments.

Within living memory, says Paul, Britain was a world leader at the design and building of reservoirs. Its water engineering and research was studied from Iran to Israel to the US. That expertise has vanished and the last big reservoir in England was built in 1992, planned and designed before privatisation.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

These financiers and their husk companies cannot cope with the scenarios laid out by scientists. This summer the water companies have urged us to take shorter showers while lobbying ministers to allow surge pricing – which means charging you and me more for our water when we most need it. Never let a good crisis go to waste, after all. Late in the day, the government has demanded the industry plan for climate breakdown, but its plans are little more than patching up leaks and cutting down on waste. As is argued in a recent book on the industry, Murky Water: Challenging an Unsustainable System, by the Foundational Economy collective, this is a “fantasy plan”, in which Thames Water and the rest suddenly fix more burst pipes than they have ever managed before.

This crisis has been in part imposed on us from above – by successive bungling governments and rapacious companies. It will not be fixed from above, by either a Labour government paralysed with fear of the electorate or financiers out to make one last buck. Even if the water industry is taken back into public hands, we will need to find a way of investing vastly more into the system. As is argued in Murky Water, the fairest way of doing that is by changing our billing system so that we pay according to our means.

But for now consider today’s Britain. A country famous for its rain struggling with a dwindling water supply. A country in the North Sea now importing its energy. A democracy that just 10 years ago voted to take back control is now on the verge of losing control over its water and energy. What a state of affairs.

Aditya Chakrabortty is a Guardian columnist

How the A. I. Borrowing Binge Helps Drive Up Government Bond Yields

The New York Times August 20, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Analysts said the recent rise in Treasury yields partly reflected investor expectations that A. I.-driven growth could keep interest rates elevated.

By Joe Rennison

Economists have been repeatedly dumbfounded by the resilience of the economy in the face of the Covid-19 pandemic, wars, tariffs, inflation and sharply higher interest rates. A simple answer has provided a catchall explanation: the growth of artificial intelligence.

But the growth of A. I. also poses a risk, reflected in the nearly two-decade highs that yields on U. S. government bonds hit this week, prompting the Treasury Department to try to put a lid on borrowing costs.

That risk stems from a borrowing binge by some of the biggest technology companies in the world. Until recently, the companies mostly self-funded the construction of data centers and other infrastructure that run their technologies. Now they are raising hundreds of billions of dollars by selling bonds to meet the voracious need for capital that advanced A. I. systems require.

“For most of the past decade, the large technology companies leading the A. I. build-out have funded their investment from operating cash flow,” said Lucas Baynes, a senior investment strategist at Vanguard. “That era is ending.”

Supercharged spending on A. I. financed in part by the surge in new bonds — over $200 billion so far this year among the largest A. I. companies — has prompted economists and investors to raise their forecasts for growth in the broader economy. Higher economic growth typically encourages the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates elevated to prevent that growth from leading to higher inflation.

Analysts said the recent rise in Treasury yields partly reflected expectations that A. I.-driven growth could push the Fed to keep rates elevated.

This week, the yield on the 30-year U. S. government bond, a benchmark for consumer loans like mortgages, rose to its highest level since 2007. The yield fell briefly after the Treasury stepped into the market on Wednesday and increased the amount of its own debt it can buy, helping to expand demand, push up prices and reduce yields. But on Thursday, yields began rising again.

That poses a problem for policymakers. The Trump administration has promised to lower borrowing costs to help improve affordability for American households, using Treasury yields as a gauge of its success.

A. I. borrowing is not the only issue pushing Treasury yields, and interest rates more broadly, higher. Analysts have also pointed to the federal deficit and the prolonged war with Iran.

But the current confluence of risks in financial markets has made the A. I. build-out a double-edged sword. While A. I. has propped up the economy with its spending, it has also contributed to a rise in interest rates, reducing affordability for borrowers, who include consumers, businesses and the government itself.

The economy “has enjoyed a massive boost” from the five so-called A. I. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle — spending their enormous stockpiles of cash to develop A. I. infrastructure, said Matt King, founder of Satori Insights, a market research firm. But that has changed, he said.

“Now that the hyperscalers are having to borrow, further capital expenditure is no longer ‘free,’” Mr. King said, meaning there is not only a cost to the company in the form of interest but also a broader cost to the economy.

“Real yields are rising, raising costs for the rest of the economy,” he added.

From 2020 to 2024, the five hyperscalers collectively issued an average of less than $30 billion in debt every year, according to data from Refinitiv. In 2025, that amount rose above $100 billion. So far this year, it has already topped $200 billion. Microsoft is the only one of the hyperscalers not to have raised money in the bond market over the past year.

Broader A. I.-related debt issuance — beyond the five hyperscalers — is expected to surpass $1 trillion annually from 2027 through 2030, according to Vanguard.

Some analysts have suggested that all this new debt is pulling investors away from the Treasury market, further raising yields on government bonds.

But others say this is likely to have only a marginal effect, given that the Treasury market is so huge and that the A. I. debt supply is having a more noticeable impact on borrowing costs in the corporate bond market.

Still, the sheer deluge of supply has been somewhat overwhelming for bond investors to absorb. And some companies have started to pay more in interest to entice investors.

The interest on corporate bonds is typically priced as a difference over the same maturity of government debt, which is known as the “spread.” Alphabet, the parent company of Google, benefits from some of the lowest corporate borrowing costs. It issued 10-year bonds in April, paying a spread of 0.63 percentage points above 10-year Treasury notes. It issued another 10-year note this month, paying a spread of 0.85 percentage points.

Amazon’s 10-year borrowing cost rose from a spread of 0.55 percentage points in November to 0.8 percentage points when it issued debt in July.

Oracle, the lowest-rated hyperscaler, paid a spread of 1.05 percentage points in September to borrow cash for 10 years. By February, investors were demanding 1.45 percentage points over Treasuries for the same-maturity debt.

The spread on a Bank of America index of investment-grade corporate bonds of similar maturities — indicative of what the average similarly rated company would pay to borrow money for 10 years — stood at just over one percentage point.

Corporate borrowing costs are rising not because investors necessarily think these companies are in trouble, said Matt Eagan, a portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles. The companies are all highly rated businesses that generate a lot of profit.

Instead, investors are struggling with the sheer amount of debt to buy, he said, from both the government and companies.

If yields are rising, prices are falling, and with no sign of the current deluge of debt slowing soon, investors are worried that the bonds they buy today will be less attractive if yields rise further.

“They’re not in danger of defaulting,” Mr. Eagan said. The concern is “about more debt coming at a cheaper price and you are left stuck holding this.”

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Elon Musk Is Expected to Point His Money Machine at Texas Politics

Wired August 19, 2026

Elon Musk is expected to spend big to boost Republicans in the midterms this November, according to Trump officials briefed on the matter.

The precise amount could change, but the officials expect Musk to spend around $100 million to $200 million with a focus on voter turnout in key races, including Texas, where the fate of Republican nominee Ken Paxton could determine which party controls the US Senate.

The planned cash injection—or any in-kind contribution relating to voter turnout—would be a boon for Paxton, who has been vastly outraised in contributions. According to the latest FEC filings, James Talarico had raised roughly $69 million compared to Paxton's $9 million.

While an endorsement from President Donald Trump carried him to victory, Paxton lagged behind in contributions throughout a bruising primary against Senator John Cornyn that resurfaced past scandals, and has fared little better since becoming the nominee.

To date, neither of the two largest national GOP entities have committed to spend on Paxton. The Senate Leadership Fund is run by allies of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who supported Cornyn, while MAGA Inc has not released its spending plans.

Democrats in close races have generally outraised their Republican counterparts this cycle, so Paxton is not unique in being behind in fundraising. Numerous candidates are relying on national party committees and outside groups to make up the difference.

Musk’s projected spend adds to the Republican National Committee’s $128 million war chest, while the Democratic National Committee is $2 million in debt. The two main GOP super PACs for House and Senate races have $380 million, compared to Democrats’ $116 million. MAGA Inc has about $400 million on hand; there is no Democratic equivalent.

A spokesperson for America PAC declined to comment on the group’s spending plans. The New York Times earlier reported that Musk had authorized his PAC to spend at least $100 million for the 2026 midterms.

But Musk's track record in setting up voter turnout operations has been mixed.

In the 2024 election, the Trump campaign outsourced its field operations to America PAC, which paid third-party canvassing firms more than $46 million across several battleground states in an attempt to turn out “low propensity” voters, who like Trump but don’t always vote.

In the end, Trump swept all six battleground states, but Trump officials were unconvinced that was a result of America PAC’s work with paid canvassers (who often are not as enthusiastic as in-house canvassers and are known to pretend to hit doors to claim their paychecks), as opposed to Trump's celebrity appeal and ability to turn out his base.

The 2024 America PAC operation also faced complaints from workers who claimed that they had been tricked, and threatened with having to pay for their own lodging unless they hit massive quotas. (America PAC and Musk did not respond to requests for comment at the time.)

I Saw the Future of AI in a Robot That Can Learn on the Spot

Wired August 19, 2026

Last week, I ventured a whopping 15 minutes from my house to see robots do some mind-boggling, jaw-dropping stuff.

I visited the Cambridge, Massachusetts, offices of a startup called Generalist AI, where I watched robot arms perform simple chores like stacking cups, putting blocks into bowls, and the like. I was astonished by how quickly they figured things out—it was reminiscent of a flesh-and-blood person.

The arms mastered a range of tasks after ingesting a short, instructional video and, most impressively, no specific training for a given task. One of the most striking examples involved a robot that was instructed to sweep a block into a bowl using a dustpan and brush. When the brush was removed from the scene, the robot improvised by using the dustpan like a brush and flicking the block into the bowl.

In another case, a two-armed robot watched a videoclip of someone unzipping a purse before removing some banknotes. I watched—somewhat slack-jawed—as the robot unzipped a different kind of purse and carefully removed the notes. Most amazingly, when it couldn’t grab the money, it switched from using its right gripper to its left to get a better angle of attack. “Ha,” said one engineer standing nearby. “It never did that before.”

“This is exactly the kind of thing people were really excited about with GPT-3,” Generalist cofounder and CEO Pete Florence told me, in reference to OpenAI’s breakthrough large language model, released in 2020. “You could take that model and just prompt it to do a new task and it would have a real shot at doing it.”

Generalist appears to be focused on teaching its robots about the physics of the world, which seems inspired by the intuitive sense of physics humans exhibit from an early age. That may well contribute to the model’s ability to transfer what it has learned in one scenario to another. In fact, some of the company’s demos made me think of how children improvise and experiment when shown a task. The researchers have often been surprised by what the robot decides to do—one chose to sweep up items with a banana when it was placed in front of it, for example. This might seem trivial, but physical intelligence is something still largely lacking in machines, and the way babies learn so efficiently about their world may offer important insights for AI researchers.

I met Florence and Andrew Barry, cofounder and CTO, in a conference room overlooking teams of people doing robot training with special grippers on their hands. The company’s other cofounder and chief scientist is Andy Zeng. The trio have impressive backgrounds: They previously worked at Google DeepMind and Boston Dynamics on some of the most advanced hardware and robotic models around.

Traditionally, training an AI-powered robot to do different tasks has meant feeding thousands of examples into the model. This is a notoriously imperfect kind of learning, though, and a robot will struggle with the task if you change something as simple as the lighting.

Generalist and some other robotics startups are investing heavily in a general robotic model trained by humans. The company builds special gloves resembling robot pincers that have cameras attached to them, which people then use to perform different chores. I saw a crate piled high with several hundred of these grippers destined for workers in Mexico and elsewhere.

Florence and team are cagey about exactly what recipe they’re using to train the robots, but they say the company has already gathered a huge amount of high-quality training data. In contrast to some other companies chasing smarter robots, they have also built their AI models entirely from scratch rather than relying on an open-source language model.

Danfei Xu, a roboticist at Georgia Tech who is familiar with Generalist’s work, says that the startup stands out among companies chasing more general robot models. “They have pushed this to the extreme, and they’ve done a really good job executing,” Xu says. Besides gathering a huge amount of high-quality data, he says, “they are excellent roboticists, and they have done really good science.”

Xu also says that the stuff Generalist has demo’d so far suggests that they have an eye on deploying robots in real commercial settings. “They are the closest to something that's deployable,” he says.

“Generalist's data approach is collecting physical interaction data at large scale without tying it too closely to one particular robot,” says Karen Liu, a roboticist at Stanford University who also knows the company. “Their strongest results suggest that this bet may be working.”

That said, Generalist says the learning skills of its models are not yet all that reliable. A robot is only able to complete a task it has been shown about 59 percent of the time, on average; ideally, its success rate would be somewhere upwards of 99 percent. It also seems unclear how well these skills will generalize to every imaginable task or setting.

Even so, the potential for robots to quickly learn skills in, say, manufacturing seems huge. One of Generalist’s engineers seemed to discover this late one recent evening. A video that captured the episode shows the engineer stacking small cups on the table in front of a two-armed robot, just to see what the machine might do. The robot suddenly joined in, grabbing and stacking other cups with its two grippers. As the robot finished stacking the cups into one neat pile, the engineer began yelling to no one in particular, delighted by the maneuver.
